meta.blurb: Arjuna drops his bow. Two armies wait, and he cannot fight the cousins and teachers he loves. His charioteer, Krishna, answers with a conversation about duty, fear and who we really are, at the heart of one of India's most loved texts.
meta.bible: Bhagavad Gita: a sacred text of Hinduism, 700 verses in 18 chapters; the name means the Song of the Lord. It is one small part of the Mahabharata, the great epic of ancient India, and is traditionally linked to the sage Vyasa. Arjuna: a Pandava prince and a great archer, brave but overcome by sorrow; Krishna's friend. Krishna: Arjuna's friend and charioteer, honoured in the tradition as the Lord himself in human form; speaks calmly, kindly and sometimes with a smile. Sanjaya: the minister who tells the whole story to the blind king, given the gift of seeing the battle from afar. Dhritarashtra: the blind king, father of the Kauravas. Kurukshetra: the plain where the armies stand. Pandavas and Kauravas: two branches of one royal family, cousins, whose armies are about to fight for the kingdom. Bhishma: the eldest and most honoured of the family. Drona: the teacher who taught Arjuna archery. Vivasvan: the sun god, to whom Krishna says he first taught this knowledge; Manu: the first lawgiver. Meru: the great mountain. Ganges: the holy river. India. Hindu. Hinduism. Sanskrit. Dharma: righteousness, the right order of things and a person's duty. Yoga: discipline, a way of joining the self with the divine. Gunas: the three strands of nature, Sattva (light, purity, calm), Rajas (passion, restlessness) and Tamas (darkness, heaviness, confusion). Self: the eternal self inside every being. Each beat is one step of the conversation, in the order of the chapters: Arjuna's despair (1), the self and duty (2), action (3), the ancient teaching (4), renunciation (5), meditation (6), knowledge (7), remembrance (8), the royal secret (9), glories (10), the universal form (11), devotion (12), the field (13), the three strands (14), the tree (15), the two natures (16), faith (17), freedom and surrender (18). Voice and tone: reverent, clear and calm; verses are paraphrased and never copied; respectful of the tradition and neutral toward other traditions; war is stated plainly and without gore; nothing is preached. Yogi: one who practises yoga. Duryodhana: the eldest Kaurava, who leads his army. Dhrishtadyumna: the Pandava commander. Karna, Kripa and Ashvatthama: warriors on the Kaurava side. Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva: Arjuna's brothers. Gandiva: Arjuna's bow. Panchajanya: Krishna's conch. Devadatta: Arjuna's conch. Hanuman: the monkey hero on Arjuna's banner. Janaka: a king of old who reached perfection through action. Brahman: the highest reality. Brahma: the creator, whose day and night are cycles of the world. Om: the sacred syllable. Veda and Vedas: the oldest sacred texts of India. Vasudeva: a name of Krishna. Purusha: the divine person. Banyan: the great fig tree of India. Himalayas: the great mountain range. Narada, Asita, Kapila: sages. Indra, Vishnu: gods of the tradition.
chapters: Teach Me, I Am Your Student
Act, but Not for the Fruit

beats.scene: A reader opens a worn book beside a small lamp
beats.summary: Introduces the Bhagavad Gita, 700 verses in 18 chapters, a conversation inside the Mahabharata.

beats.scene: Two armies of cousins face each other beneath a painted family tree
beats.summary: The Mahabharata tells how two sets of cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, came to fight over a kingdom.

beats.scene: A blind king on a palace terrace turns his face toward his minister
beats.summary: Blind King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas are doing at Kurukshetra.

beats.scene: A minister sits calmly while a shining vision of a battlefield fills the air
beats.summary: Sanjaya, by the gift of the sage Vyasa, sees the whole field from afar and reports it to the king.

beats.scene: Prince Duryodhana walks toward his teacher Drona as two armies fill a dusty plain
beats.summary: Duryodhana tells Drona to look at the Pandava army, arranged by Drona's own gifted pupil.

beats.scene: Duryodhana names his great commanders while a white-haired elder watches over them
beats.summary: Duryodhana lists the heroes on his side and orders them all to guard Bhishma.

beats.scene: Old Bhishma lifts a great shell to his lips and the whole army cheers
beats.summary: Bhishma, the eldest of the family, roars like a lion and blows his conch to cheer Duryodhana.

beats.scene: Drums, horns and shells all sound at once above a huge army
beats.summary: Conches, kettledrums, tabors and horns suddenly blare out across the Kuru army in a tremendous din.

beats.scene: Krishna and Arjuna in a white-horse chariot blow their shining conches
beats.summary: In their great chariot with white horses, Krishna and Arjuna answer by blowing their divine conches.

beats.scene: Five brothers stand in their chariots and sound their shells across the plain
beats.summary: The other Pandava brothers also blow their conches, and the roar shakes the hearts of the Kauravas.

beats.scene: A banner of the monkey hero Hanuman flies over an archer raising his bow
beats.summary: Arjuna sees the Kaurava army ready to fight and asks Krishna to halt the chariot between the two armies.

beats.scene: Krishna stops the white horses in the open space facing Bhishma and Drona
beats.summary: Krishna drives to the middle of the field, in front of Bhishma and Drona, and tells Arjuna to look.

beats.scene: Arjuna looks along rows of grey-haired elders, uncles, cousins and old friends
beats.summary: Arjuna sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and friends standing on both sides.

beats.scene: Arjuna grips the chariot rail with a pale face and trembling hands
beats.summary: Overcome by pity, Arjuna says his limbs fail, his mouth is dry and his body shakes.

beats.scene: A great bow slips from Arjuna's hand and he sways in the chariot
beats.summary: The bow Gandiva slips from his hand, his skin burns, his mind whirls and he sees bad signs.

beats.scene: Arjuna turns to Krishna with open, empty hands
beats.summary: Arjuna sees no good in killing his own family and asks what use a kingdom would be to them.

beats.scene: Arjuna looks out at the armies and shakes his head
beats.summary: He would not kill them even to rule the three worlds, and killing the Kauravas could bring only sorrow.

beats.scene: An old family gathers around a fire, and the fire begins to die
beats.summary: Arjuna fears that destroying a family also destroys the customs and duties that hold it together.

beats.scene: Arjuna stares at the field with a heavy, troubled face
beats.summary: Arjuna grieves that they are ready to do a great wrong, driven by the greed for a kingdom.

beats.scene: Arjuna sits in the chariot with his bow and arrows set aside
beats.summary: Arjuna says it would be better to be killed unarmed, throws down his bow and sits in sorrow.

beats.scene: Krishna looks gently at the weeping Arjuna as two armies wait
beats.summary: Krishna asks where this weakness has come from at such a moment, and tells Arjuna to stand up.

beats.scene: Arjuna looks across at the two white-haired men he has honoured all his life
beats.summary: Arjuna asks how he can shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, who deserve his respect.

beats.scene: A beggar's bowl rests beside a bow on the floor of a chariot
beats.summary: Arjuna says he would rather live on alms than win wealth stained with the blood of his teachers.

beats.scene: Arjuna spreads his empty hands, unable to choose between two kinds of loss
beats.summary: Arjuna cannot say whether winning or losing would be better, since those he would kill stand before him.

beats.scene: Arjuna bows his head to Krishna like a pupil to a teacher
beats.summary: Confused about his duty, Arjuna asks Krishna to teach him and says he is Krishna's student.

beats.scene: A golden crown and a heap of coins lie unwanted at Arjuna's feet
beats.summary: Arjuna says even a rich kingdom or the rule of the gods could not take away his sorrow.

beats.scene: Arjuna sits with his head down and the silence stretches between the two armies
beats.summary: Arjuna tells Krishna he will not fight, and then he falls silent.

beats.scene: Krishna smiles warmly at Arjuna in the quiet space between the armies
beats.summary: Smiling, Krishna begins to speak to the sorrowful Arjuna in the middle of the two armies.

beats.scene: A wise old teacher sits calmly beside a sorrowful young man
beats.summary: Krishna says Arjuna grieves for those who should not be grieved for, while the wise grieve for neither living nor dead.

beats.scene: A child, a young man and an old man stand in a line
beats.summary: Krishna says no one has ever ceased to be, and that the self passes through childhood, youth and age and then into another body.

beats.scene: A man stands steady in turn through snow, rain and summer sun
beats.summary: Krishna says heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, so Arjuna must bear them calmly.

beats.scene: A tall wave rises and falls on a wide, still ocean
beats.summary: Krishna says the unreal has no lasting being while the real never ceases, and what fills the whole world cannot be destroyed.

beats.scene: Krishna lifts a hand toward the sky above the two waiting armies
beats.summary: Bodies come to an end but the self does not, so the one who thinks he kills and the one who thinks he is killed are both mistaken.

beats.scene: A single bright star shines unmoving over a dark hill
beats.summary: The self is never born and never dies; it is unborn, eternal and ancient, and it is not killed when the body is killed.

beats.scene: A sword, a flame, a stream and the wind pass a calm glowing figure
beats.summary: Weapons cannot cut the self, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it and wind cannot dry it.

beats.scene: A man changes from worn clothes into fresh white clothes
beats.summary: As a person puts on new clothes and throws away the old, so the self takes on new bodies.

beats.scene: A sage with closed eyes sits quietly before a veil of mist
beats.summary: The self cannot be seen, cannot be grasped by thought and does not change, so Arjuna should not grieve.

beats.scene: Two paths curve around a hill, one leading in and one leading out
beats.summary: Even if Arjuna thinks the self is born and dies again and again, death is certain for the born and birth for the dead.

beats.scene: A morning mist lifts from a valley and thin clouds soon return
beats.summary: Beings are unseen before birth, seen in the middle and unseen again after death, so Krishna asks why anyone should mourn.

beats.scene: A traveller stops on a mountain path and gazes at a sunrise in wonder
beats.summary: Some see the self as a wonder, others speak of it as a wonder, and the one in every body can never be killed.

beats.scene: A warrior in a chariot faces an open golden doorway in the sky
beats.summary: Krishna says a warrior has no better duty than a righteous war, and such a battle is like an open door to heaven.

beats.scene: A warrior turns away from a banner lying in the dust
beats.summary: If Arjuna refuses this fair fight, Krishna says, he will give up his duty and his good name.

beats.scene: Crowds whisper behind the back of a lone warrior walking away
beats.summary: People will speak of his shame forever, and for an honoured man shame is worse than death.

beats.scene: Great chariot fighters talk in a group and point at Arjuna
beats.summary: The great warriors will think he left the field out of fear, and enemies will say cruel things about him.

beats.scene: Two roads lead to a sunlit hill and a green plain
beats.summary: If Arjuna is killed he reaches heaven, and if he wins he enjoys the earth, so he should rise and fight.

beats.scene: A level balance scale holds a gold coin and a plain stone
beats.summary: Krishna says Arjuna should treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat alike, and then no sin will touch him.

beats.scene: A teacher draws two paths in the sand and points to the second
beats.summary: Krishna says he has explained the wisdom of knowing the self, and now he will explain the wisdom of acting, which cuts the bonds of action.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a long road with a small lamp that never goes out
beats.summary: On this path no effort is wasted and nothing is lost, and even a little of this practice protects from great fear.

beats.scene: One straight arrow flies ahead while a scatter of arrows flies in every direction
beats.summary: A resolved mind has one aim, but the minds of the undecided branch out in endless directions.

beats.scene: A crowd listens to a speaker with flowery words and a jewelled robe
beats.summary: Some people use flowery words and long for pleasure and power, so their minds cannot rest in a firm decision.

beats.scene: Three coloured threads twist together while a calm figure steps free of them
beats.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna to rise above the three strands of nature and the pairs of opposites, and to stay steady in the self.

beats.scene: A farmer scatters seed across a field at sunrise
beats.summary: Krishna says Arjuna has a right to his actions but never to their fruits.

beats.scene: A hand holds a bow lightly beside an empty idle seat
beats.summary: Arjuna must not act for results, and must not cling to doing nothing either; he must act with an even mind.

beats.scene: A worker carves a small wooden bowl with great care and no audience
beats.summary: Action done for reward is lower than action done with a steady mind, and yoga is skill in action.

beats.scene: A traveller steps out of a thick thorny thicket into an open meadow
beats.summary: Wise people free themselves from the bondage of rebirth, and when the mind leaves the thicket of confusion it finds a settled peace.

beats.scene: Arjuna leans forward in his chariot with a puzzled look
beats.summary: Arjuna asks how a person of steady wisdom speaks, sits and walks.

beats.scene: A man sits happily alone under a tree with nothing in his hands
beats.summary: Krishna says the steady person gives up every desire of the mind and is content in the self.

beats.scene: A calm man stands still in a storm while the others rush past
beats.summary: The wise are not shaken by sorrow, do not crave pleasure and are free from fear and anger.

beats.scene: A tortoise draws in its legs and rests in its shell
beats.summary: Like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, the steady person draws the senses back from their objects.

beats.scene: A man at a feast turns his plate away as a tempting smell remains
beats.summary: Even if a person turns away from sense objects, the taste for them remains until the highest is seen.

beats.scene: A charioteer holds tight reins as wild horses pull in every direction
beats.summary: Krishna says the restless senses can carry away even a wise person's mind, so they must be held in control.

beats.scene: A man gazes longingly at a glittering jewel in a market stall
beats.summary: Brooding on the objects of the senses leads to attachment, attachment to desire and desire to anger.

beats.scene: A stormy sky darkens over a traveller stumbling on a narrow road
beats.summary: Anger leads to confusion, confusion to loss of memory and loss of reason, and loss of reason brings ruin.

beats.scene: A clear pool grows still until it reflects the whole sky
beats.summary: A person who moves among objects with a controlled mind, free of like and dislike, finds a serene calm that ends sorrow.

beats.scene: A candle flickers in a draught beside a sleepless man
beats.summary: Without discipline there is no steady wisdom, and without peace there can be no happiness.

beats.scene: A small ship tosses on grey waves under a strong wind
beats.summary: As wind carries a ship off its course, a wandering sense can carry away the mind.

beats.scene: A sage sits awake beneath the stars while a village sleeps
beats.summary: What is night for most beings is wakefulness for the wise, and what others call waking is night for the sage.

beats.scene: Rivers pour into a wide ocean that stays calm and unmoved
beats.summary: The one into whom all desires flow as rivers flow into the sea, and is not disturbed, finds peace.

beats.scene: A traveller sets down a heavy bundle at the end of a long road
beats.summary: The one who gives up all longing and lives without ego and ownership attains peace.

beats.scene: The evening light warms the plain as Arjuna listens in the chariot
beats.summary: This is the state of union with Brahman; reached even at the end of life, it brings freedom.

beats.scene: Arjuna frowns at Krishna with his hands raised in confusion
beats.summary: Arjuna asks why Krishna urges him to act if knowledge is higher than action, and says his words seem to confuse him.

beats.scene: A scholar reads in a library while a farmer works the field outside
beats.summary: Krishna says there are two paths, knowledge for those who reflect and action for those who work.

beats.scene: A man sits perfectly still, but his eyes follow a passing bird
beats.summary: No one can rest from action even for a moment, and a person who only pretends to restrain the senses is deceiving himself.

beats.scene: A wheel turns as people pass baskets of grain from hand to hand
beats.summary: Krishna describes the wheel of giving, in which work offered as a sacrifice sustains the world, and the one who only takes is a thief.

beats.scene: A great king in simple robes rules his city while a crowd watches
beats.summary: Kings like Janaka reached perfection through action, and whatever a great person does, the world follows.

beats.scene: Krishna stands in a field of light as the world turns behind him
beats.summary: Krishna says he has nothing to gain in the three worlds, yet he acts, for if he stopped, the world would fall.

beats.scene: A teacher works patiently beside a pupil who does not yet understand
beats.summary: The wise act without attachment for the good of the world, and they do not confuse those who have not yet understood.

beats.scene: A potter at his wheel and a weaver at his loom nearby
beats.summary: Even the wise act according to their nature; Krishna says it is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than another's well.

beats.scene: Arjuna leans forward with a troubled face and asks his question
beats.summary: Arjuna asks what drives a person to do wrong, even against his will, and Krishna says it is desire and anger.

beats.scene: Dark smoke covers a bright fire while dust gathers on a mirror
beats.summary: Desire covers wisdom as smoke covers fire and dust covers a mirror; mind and intellect must master the senses.

beats.scene: A glowing scroll passes from the sun god to a king
beats.summary: Krishna says he taught this ancient yoga to Vivasvan, who told Manu, and that it was lost in time, so he teaches it again to his friend.

beats.scene: Arjuna tilts his head in surprise while Krishna smiles beside him
beats.summary: Arjuna asks how Krishna could have taught Vivasvan, who lived long before, and Krishna says he remembers many births.

beats.scene: A bright light rises over a dim town as people look up
beats.summary: Whenever righteousness declines, Krishna says, he comes into the world to protect the good and restore dharma.

beats.scene: Many roads climb different slopes toward one shining peak
beats.summary: One who truly knows the divine birth and work is freed from rebirth, and Krishna welcomes all who come to him in any way.

beats.scene: People bring offerings to many shrines in a busy temple courtyard
beats.summary: Those who want quick success worship the powers of nature, but Krishna's own actions never touch him, and the wise of old knew this.

beats.scene: A boatman rows quietly across a still lake
beats.summary: Even the wise are puzzled by what is action and what is inaction, and Krishna says the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction.

beats.scene: A man works quietly in a field with a calm, contented face
beats.summary: The wise person has no desire in his undertakings, is content with whatever comes and is free from envy, and acts without being bound.

beats.scene: A priest, a teacher and a giver make different offerings around one fire
beats.summary: There are many kinds of sacrifice, such as giving, discipline, study and control of breath, and the sacrifice of knowledge is greater than any gift of things.

beats.scene: A small boat crosses a wide dark river toward a bright shore
beats.summary: Krishna advises Arjuna to seek wise teachers, to ask with humility and to serve them, for knowledge is a boat that carries even a sinner across.

beats.scene: A glowing sword of light rises beside Arjuna in the chariot
beats.summary: Knowledge burns up the bonds of action like fire burns wood, and Krishna tells Arjuna to cut his doubt with the sword of knowledge and stand up.

beats.scene: Arjuna leans toward Krishna with two small signposts pointing in opposite directions
beats.summary: Arjuna asks whether giving up action or practising action is better, and Krishna says both lead to the highest, but acting is the better way.

beats.scene: A child points at two roads while a wise man smiles
beats.summary: The true renouncer neither hates nor desires, and only children see knowledge and action as two different paths.

beats.scene: A man walks calmly through a loud market among stalls of fruit and cloth
beats.summary: The wise person knows that the senses move among their objects, so he thinks, I do nothing at all, even as he sees, hears and walks.

beats.scene: Water drops roll off a lotus leaf in a still pond
beats.summary: One who acts, offering actions to the highest and giving up attachment, is untouched by wrong, like a lotus leaf in water.

beats.scene: Dawn light breaks over a walled city with nine gates
beats.summary: The self rests in the body like a king in a city of nine gates, and knowledge shines like the sun on ignorance.

beats.scene: A scholar, a cow, an elephant and a dog rest beneath one tree
beats.summary: The wise see with an equal eye all beings, a learned person, a cow, an elephant or a dog.

beats.scene: A traveller stands calm between a bright feast and an empty table
beats.summary: The one who is not carried away by pleasure or pain, and masters desire and anger, is truly happy.

beats.scene: A person sits happy and quiet with a small lamp glowing in the chest
beats.summary: The yogi finds joy and light within, and one who knows Krishna as the friend of all beings finds peace.

beats.scene: A man lifts a small fire from the ground and holds it carefully
beats.summary: The true renouncer works without depending on results, and for one who is learning, action is the way, while for the advanced, stillness is.

beats.scene: Gold, a stone and clay lie side by side before a calm man
beats.summary: Lift yourself by your own effort, for the self is its own friend or enemy, and the yogi sees gold, stone and clay as equal.

beats.scene: A yogi spreads a simple grass seat in a quiet clearing
beats.summary: Krishna describes how a yogi should practise: alone, in a clean and quiet place, on a firm seat, with a still and focused mind.

beats.scene: A man sits upright and still in a forest clearing at dawn
beats.summary: The yogi sits with his body upright and steady, his gaze quiet, fearless and calm, and his mind fixed on Krishna, and he finds peace.

beats.scene: A balanced scale holds a bowl of rice and a pillow
beats.summary: Yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little; moderation in everything ends sorrow.

beats.scene: A small oil lamp burns without a flicker in a still room
beats.summary: A mind that rests in the self is like a lamp in a windless place, and does not flicker.

beats.scene: A meditating figure glows quietly while a storm passes outside
beats.summary: The yogi finds a joy beyond the senses, and having found it he is not shaken even by great sorrow.

beats.scene: A shepherd gently leads a wandering lamb back to the flock
beats.summary: Whenever the restless mind wanders, the yogi should bring it back gently under the control of the self.

beats.scene: A person gazes at a crowd and sees one soft light in every face
beats.summary: The best yogi sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and feels the joy and the pain of others as his own.

beats.scene: A swirl of leaves blows across a courtyard past a student
beats.summary: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna says it can be held by practice and detachment.

beats.scene: A fallen traveller rises with a helping hand and walks on
beats.summary: Arjuna asks what happens to a sincere seeker who fails, and Krishna says no good effort is ever lost.

beats.scene: A climber reaches a high ridge at sunrise after a long journey
beats.summary: After many births a yogi can reach the highest goal, and Krishna tells Arjuna to be a yogi.

beats.scene: A crowd at the foot of a mountain while a few begin to climb
beats.summary: Krishna promises to teach knowledge with experience, and says that among thousands of people few strive, and among those few hardly one knows him truly.

beats.scene: Pearls on a golden thread glow in the lamplight
beats.summary: Krishna describes his eightfold nature of earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego, and says all things are strung on him like pearls on a thread.

beats.scene: A clear glass of water and a full moon shine over a quiet lake
beats.summary: Krishna says he is the taste in water, the light of the moon and sun, the sacred sound Om, the fragrance of earth and the life in all beings.

beats.scene: A traveller crosses a river of mist on a narrow bridge of light
beats.summary: The three strands of nature come from Krishna, and this divine illusion is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him cross it.

beats.scene: A tired woman, a student, a merchant and an old man kneel at dawn
beats.summary: Four kinds of good people worship Krishna: the distressed, the seekers of knowledge, the seekers of wealth and the wise, and the wise are dearest to him.

beats.scene: People kneel at different shrines beneath one wide sky
beats.summary: Krishna steadies the faith of those who worship other powers, but he is hidden by his divine power, and only those who seek him steadily find him.

beats.scene: Arjuna counts questions on his fingers while Krishna listens
beats.summary: Arjuna asks seven questions about Brahman, the self, action and the meaning of death, and Krishna begins to answer them.

beats.scene: A traveller at a mountain pass looks back at a glowing sunset
beats.summary: Whatever one remembers at the hour of death is what one reaches, so Krishna tells Arjuna to remember him always and to fight.

beats.scene: A great wheel of day and night turns slowly above the mountains
beats.summary: Krishna says worlds rise and fall in great cycles of day and night, but beyond them there is an eternal existence that does not perish.

beats.scene: A bright road and a dim road lead out of a valley at dusk
beats.summary: Krishna speaks of two paths after death, one of light and one of darkness, and says the yogi who knows them is not confused.

beats.scene: Krishna leans close to Arjuna as if sharing a secret
beats.summary: Krishna offers Arjuna the royal secret, a knowledge that is direct, joyful to practise and supremely purifying.

beats.scene: A great wind moves freely through an open sky
beats.summary: Krishna says the whole world rests in him, as the mighty wind rests in space, yet he is not limited by the world.

beats.scene: A river of creatures flows out of a golden dawn and back into dusk
beats.summary: Beings return to Krishna's nature at the end of an age and are sent forth again, and he is not bound by this, as he sits like a witness.

beats.scene: A crowd walks past a humble stranger without noticing him
beats.summary: Fools disregard Krishna when he takes a human form, but great souls worship him with undivided minds.

beats.scene: Rain falls on a field in the summer sun
beats.summary: Krishna says he is the ritual, the offering, the father, the mother, the friend, the refuge, the heat of the sun and the rain.

beats.scene: A guardian lifts a small lantern beside a trusting traveller
beats.summary: Those who seek only rewards return again and again, but Krishna provides and protects for those who think only of him.

beats.scene: A girl offers a leaf, a flower and water at a shrine
beats.summary: Krishna accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with love and a pure heart.

beats.scene: A cook sets a warm bowl of food before a small shrine
beats.summary: Whatever one does, eats, gives or practises, Krishna says, should be done as an offering, and this frees one from bondage.

beats.scene: Warm light falls on a man with a bowed head at a temple door
beats.summary: Krishna is equal to all, and even the worst sinner who turns to him with full devotion is soon made righteous.

beats.scene: A crowd of every kind of people walks toward one lit doorway
beats.summary: People of every background can reach the highest goal, so Arjuna should fix his mind on Krishna and be devoted to him.

beats.scene: Krishna speaks to Arjuna as clouds roll slowly across the plain
beats.summary: Krishna offers Arjuna a supreme word, and says that neither gods nor sages know his origin, since he is their source.

beats.scene: A great tree with many branches grows from a single root
beats.summary: Every quality of living beings, such as wisdom, forgiveness, courage and fear, comes from Krishna, and he is the source of everything.

beats.scene: Friends sit together by a lamp and talk quietly late into the night
beats.summary: Devotees fix their minds on Krishna, talk of him together and are content, and he lights the lamp of knowledge in their hearts.

beats.scene: Arjuna bows with folded hands as the clouds part above him
beats.summary: Arjuna praises Krishna as the supreme reality, as the sages declare, and asks him to describe his divine glories.

beats.scene: A small light glows inside a figure sitting quietly
beats.summary: Krishna says he is the self in every heart, and the beginning, the middle and the end of all beings.

beats.scene: Snow peaks, a great ocean and the moon rise together in a golden sky
beats.summary: Among lights Krishna is the sun, among stars the moon, among mountains Meru and among waters the ocean.

beats.scene: A banyan tree, a lion and a river meet in a quiet clearing
beats.summary: Among trees Krishna is the banyan, among beasts the lion, among rivers the Ganges and among men the king.

beats.scene: Spring blossoms open across a green hillside
beats.summary: Among seasons Krishna is spring, and he is also the splendour of the splendid, victory, effort and the goodness of the good.

beats.scene: A sage writes by lamplight while a lone archer stands outside in the dark
beats.summary: Among the Pandavas Krishna is Arjuna, among sages Vyasa, and among secrets he is silence and among the wise, wisdom.

beats.scene: A tiny spark lights up a sky filled with countless stars
beats.summary: There is no end to Krishna's glories; a single fragment of himself holds up the whole universe.

beats.scene: Arjuna bows to Krishna with folded hands in the chariot
beats.summary: Arjuna says his confusion is gone and asks Krishna to show him his divine form, if he thinks Arjuna can bear to see it.

beats.scene: Krishna touches Arjuna's brow as a faint golden light begins to glow
beats.summary: Krishna says Arjuna cannot see his form with ordinary eyes, so he gives him a divine eye.

beats.scene: A blazing universe of countless faces, eyes and lights fills the sky
beats.summary: Sanjaya tells the king that Krishna shows his supreme form, with countless mouths, eyes and weapons and a light like a thousand suns.

beats.scene: Gods, sages and countless beings appear inside a vast shining body
beats.summary: Arjuna sees all the gods, sages and beings within Krishna's body, with no beginning, middle or end.

beats.scene: A vast glowing figure touches the sky while the mountains below tremble
beats.summary: Arjuna sees a being with endless arms, with the sun and moon for eyes, and the three worlds tremble at the sight.

beats.scene: Great fiery mouths open across a darkening sky above a trembling archer
beats.summary: Arjuna cries that his courage and peace have left him, and he begs Krishna to be merciful.

beats.scene: Streams rush into a wide ocean and moths fly toward a flame
beats.summary: Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies rushing into the blazing mouths, like rivers into the sea and moths into a flame, and asks who Krishna is.

beats.scene: A great wheel of time turns above the two armies
beats.summary: Krishna says he is Time, the destroyer of worlds, and that the warriors are already slain by him, so Arjuna should be merely his instrument.

beats.scene: Arjuna kneels in the chariot with joined hands and tears on his face
beats.summary: Arjuna praises Krishna, asks forgiveness for calling him a mere friend, and begs to see his gentle human form again.

beats.scene: The light fades as Krishna's gentle human face returns
beats.summary: Krishna says he showed this form by his grace, then calms Arjuna's fear and returns to his gentle human form.

beats.scene: Arjuna breathes out with relief as Krishna sits beside him with a gentle smile
beats.summary: Arjuna says that seeing Krishna's gentle form calms his mind, and Krishna says even the gods long to see the form he has just shown.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a quiet path toward a soft light
beats.summary: Krishna says this vision cannot be won by study, gifts or rituals, but only by single-minded devotion, work for his sake and love for all beings.

beats.scene: Two people pray, one before a statue and one before an empty sky
beats.summary: Arjuna asks whether those who worship Krishna with devotion or those who worship the formless are better yogis, and Krishna says those devoted to him are best.

beats.scene: A rescuer pulls a swimmer from a stormy sea
beats.summary: Those who worship the formless also reach Krishna, but the way is harder, and Krishna quickly lifts his devotees from the ocean of birth and death.

beats.scene: A staircase of four steps rises toward a bright door
beats.summary: Krishna gives steps for every ability: fix your mind on me, or practise, or work for me, or at least give up the fruits of your actions.

beats.scene: A gentle woman greets a friend and a stranger with the same warm smile
beats.summary: Krishna describes the devotee who is dear to him: hating no one, friendly, humble, forgiving, steady in pleasure and pain, and equal in praise and blame.

beats.scene: A farmer crosses a wide field as a watcher sits on a hill
beats.summary: Krishna says the body is the field and the one who knows it is the knower of the field.

beats.scene: A busy village with market stalls, paths and a quiet watchtower
beats.summary: The field includes the elements, the senses, the mind, desire, pleasure, pain and the will, which change constantly.

beats.scene: A humble student bows to a teacher and hands him a jug of water
beats.summary: True knowledge is humility, non-violence, patience, honesty, service to the teacher, self-control and steady devotion.

beats.scene: A single flame is reflected in the eyes of many faces
beats.summary: What is to be known is the highest reality, without beginning, near and far, the light of all lights, seated in every heart.

beats.scene: A silent witness sits above a busy loom of many colours
beats.summary: Nature and the spirit have no beginning; nature acts, while the supreme in the body is the witness who permits, supports and experiences.

beats.scene: Four travellers climb four different paths up one mountain
beats.summary: Some seek the self by meditation, some by knowledge, some by action, some by faith in what they hear, and the one who sees the Lord equally in all beings does not harm himself.

beats.scene: The sun lights a whole valley while a clear blue sky stays untouched
beats.summary: Nature does the action, space is never stained, and as one sun lights the whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field.

beats.scene: A seed sprouts in dark soil under a quiet sky
beats.summary: Krishna says the great Brahman is the womb in which he places the seed, and all beings are born from it.

beats.scene: Three lamps of different brightness glow in a quiet dark room
beats.summary: Nature has three strands: sattva, bright and calm, rajas, restless and passionate, and tamas, dark and dull, and each binds in its own way.

beats.scene: A ladder, a crowded road and a downward slope lie side by side
beats.summary: Each strand rises by overcoming the others, and each leads to its own result: upward, to the middle, and downward.

beats.scene: A calm man holds a lump of gold and a lump of clay equally
beats.summary: One who sees beyond the three strands is the same in praise and blame, in gold and clay, and finds immortality through devotion.

beats.scene: A huge banyan tree with its roots in the sky and its branches below
beats.summary: Krishna describes the world as a great tree with roots above, to be cut by the strong axe of detachment, so that one may find the goal from which there is no return.

beats.scene: A small spark of light drifts from one body to another
beats.summary: A portion of Krishna lives as the self in each being, and when it leaves one body it carries the mind and senses to the next, as the wind carries scent.

beats.scene: Warm sunlight, a hearth fire and a moonlit night glow around one quiet heart
beats.summary: Krishna says the light of the sun, moon and fire is his, he sits in every heart, and he is the highest person beyond the perishable and imperishable.

beats.scene: Lanterns of different colours glow along one side of a path
beats.summary: Krishna lists the divine qualities, among them fearlessness, purity, charity, self-control, truth, gentleness, compassion, forgiveness and freedom from pride.

beats.scene: Two paths, one lit by bright lamps and the other dark with thorns
beats.summary: Hypocrisy, arrogance, anger and harshness belong to the ungodly nature; divine qualities lead to freedom and ungodly ones to bondage, and Arjuna has divine qualities.

beats.scene: A rich man counts his coins while long shadows grow behind him
beats.summary: Krishna describes people who think only of wealth and pleasure and say, I am the lord, who is equal to me, and so fall into confusion.

beats.scene: A traveller stands before three heavy dark gates that are tightly closed
beats.summary: Desire, anger and greed are three gates to ruin, so Arjuna should give them up and let scripture guide what he does.

beats.scene: Three people pray in different ways at one old shrine
beats.summary: Arjuna asks about those who have faith but ignore the rules, and Krishna says faith is of three kinds, following one's nature.

beats.scene: A man sits painfully on thorns while a gentle person watches with concern
beats.summary: Krishna says those who harm their bodies with harsh discipline out of pride are mistaken, for they trouble the divine presence within.

beats.scene: A table with three plates of food: plain, spicy and stale
beats.summary: Krishna describes three kinds of food, the light and nourishing, the harsh and burning, and the stale and tasteless, each liked by a different nature.

beats.scene: A quiet family shares a meal while a loud man performs for a crowd
beats.summary: A sacrifice done as a duty with no wish for reward is the best, while one done for show or reward is lower.

beats.scene: A teacher speaks softly and truthfully to a student who listens carefully
beats.summary: Discipline of the body is respect and non-violence, discipline of speech is truthful, kind and helpful words, and discipline of the mind is calm and purity of heart.

beats.scene: A hand quietly gives a bowl of grain to a stranger
beats.summary: The best gift is given from duty, without hope of return, and Om Tat Sat marks any act done with faith; without faith, acts are worthless.

beats.scene: Arjuna sits with folded hands and his bow resting beside him
beats.summary: Arjuna asks Krishna to explain renunciation and relinquishment, and Krishna says the wise call giving up the fruits of action true relinquishment.

beats.scene: A potter's hands shape a clay pot steadily and calmly
beats.summary: Krishna says sacrifice, giving and discipline should never be given up, for they purify the wise, but they should be done without attachment to results.

beats.scene: One man throws down his tool in frustration while another lifts it calmly
beats.summary: Giving up duty from confusion or from fear of effort is poor renunciation; doing duty without attachment is best, and no one can give up all action.

beats.scene: Five hands hold one rope to pull a boat toward the shore
beats.summary: Krishna names five causes of any action, and says that one who thinks the self alone is the doer does not see rightly.

beats.scene: One person sees a forest, another sees trees and a third sees one leaf
beats.summary: Knowledge is of three kinds: seeing one reality in all beings, seeing many separate things, or clinging to one small thing as if it were everything.

beats.scene: Three builders work side by side: one calm, one frantic and one half asleep
beats.summary: Action and the doer are also of three kinds, depending on calm, passion or darkness, and Krishna describes each in turn.

beats.scene: A traveller at a crossroads reads the signposts by clear morning light
beats.summary: Intellect and steadiness come in three kinds, and the best knows what to do and what to avoid, what to fear and what not to fear.

beats.scene: A student studies by lamplight while a friend eats sweets at a stall
beats.summary: Happiness is of three kinds: bitter at first and sweet at the end, sweet at first and bitter at the end, or empty from beginning to end.

beats.scene: A teacher, a warrior, a farmer and a craftsman stand by their tools
beats.summary: No being is free from the three strands, and Krishna says each person has duties that suit his nature, in the language of the Gita's time.

beats.scene: A potter at his wheel and a weaver at his loom
beats.summary: Each person reaches perfection by honouring the divine through his own work, and it is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than another's well.

beats.scene: A man sits in a quiet hut at dawn with a simple meal
beats.summary: A person with a detached mind reaches freedom, and the steps are a pure mind, firm will, simple living, control of speech and body, meditation and freedom from ego and desire.

beats.scene: A calm person looks across a crowd with a gentle smile
beats.summary: Having become Brahman, the person is serene, neither grieves nor craves, sees all beings alike, and by devotion knows Krishna truly.

beats.scene: Arjuna lifts his face as Krishna's hand rests lightly on the reins
beats.summary: Krishna says that by his grace even a person who acts in all ways reaches the eternal home, so Arjuna should surrender his actions to him and listen.

beats.scene: Arjuna looks at his hands as his fallen bow lies in the chariot
beats.summary: Krishna says that if Arjuna refuses to fight out of ego, his own nature will compel him, since the Lord lives in the hearts of all.

beats.scene: Krishna opens his hands to Arjuna as the two sit quietly in the chariot
beats.summary: Krishna asks Arjuna to take refuge in him, says he has told him the most secret knowledge, and tells him to think it over and then do as he wishes.

beats.scene: Arjuna bows with folded hands as a golden light touches the chariot
beats.summary: Krishna gives his supreme word: let go of every other support and take refuge in him alone, and he will free Arjuna from all fear and sorrow.

beats.scene: A teacher shares a worn book with a few quiet listeners at dusk
beats.summary: Krishna says whom to share this teaching with, and that those who teach it, study it or listen to it with faith are blessed.

beats.scene: Arjuna stands calm in his chariot with his bow raised again
beats.summary: Krishna asks if Arjuna has listened with a single mind, and Arjuna says his confusion is gone, his doubts are over and he will do as Krishna says.

beats.scene: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king in a lamplit hall
beats.summary: Sanjaya tells the king that he heard the whole wonderful conversation, and that remembering it again and again fills him with joy.

beats.scene: A reader closes the worn book beside the small lamp
beats.summary: Sanjaya says that where Krishna and Arjuna are, there will be good fortune and victory, and the Gita closes as a conversation that is still read today.

A1A2: The Bhagavad Gita is a holy book from India, and it is very old.
Two families of cousins lived in one kingdom, and both wanted to rule it.
A blind king asked his helper Sanjaya what was happening at the battle.
Sanjaya had a special gift, so he could see the battlefield far away.
Prince Duryodhana went to his teacher Drona and pointed at the other army.
Duryodhana named his best fighters and told them to protect old Bhishma.
Old Bhishma blew his great shell, and the whole army shouted with joy.
Then drums and horns began to sound, and the noise was very loud.
Krishna and Arjuna rode in a great chariot with white horses.
The brothers of Arjuna also blew their shells, and the noise shook the Kauravas' hearts.
Arjuna raised his bow, and he asked Krishna to stop between the armies.
Krishna drove into the middle of the field and said, “Look, Arjuna.”
Arjuna saw his uncles, teachers, cousins and friends on both sides.
Arjuna felt weak, his mouth was dry, and his body began to shake.
His great bow fell from his hand, and he could not stand up.
Arjuna said that no kingdom could make him happy after this.
He did not want to kill his family, even to rule the world.
Arjuna thought that when a family is destroyed, its good ways are lost.
He was sad because they were ready to do something very wrong for a kingdom.
Arjuna threw down his bow and sat down in the chariot with tears.
Krishna asked Arjuna, “Why has this weakness come to you now?”
Arjuna said he could not shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona.
He said it was better to beg for food than to kill his teachers.
Arjuna did not know whether winning or losing would be better.
He felt lost, so he asked Krishna to teach him like a student.
Even a rich kingdom could not take away the sorrow in his heart.
Arjuna told Krishna, “I will not fight,” and then he was quiet.
Krishna smiled kindly and began to speak to the sad prince.
Krishna said the wise are not sad about the living or the dead.
Krishna said we were always alive, and we will always be alive.
Krishna said heat and cold, joy and pain, all come and go.
What is real never ends, and nothing can destroy it.
The body ends, but the self inside us does not end.
The self is never born, and the self never dies.
No sword can cut the self, and no fire can burn it.
A person puts on new clothes, and the self takes a new body.
Nobody can see the self, and it never changes, so do not be sad.
Even then, everyone who is born must die, so there is no need to cry.
Beings cannot be seen before birth or after death, so why weep?
Some people see the self as a wonder, and the self cannot be killed.
For a warrior, a fair fight is a door to heaven.
If you refuse this fight, you will lose your duty and your good name.
People will talk about your shame forever, and shame is worse than death.
The great warriors will think you ran away from fear.
If you die, you reach heaven, and if you win, you rule the earth.
Treat joy and pain, gain and loss, and winning and losing the same.
Krishna said, “I have taught you about knowledge, and now I will teach you about action.”
On this path no effort is lost, and even a little keeps you safe.
A firm mind has one aim, but a doubting mind goes in many directions.
Some people use fancy words and want only pleasure, so their minds are never calm.
Krishna said, “Do not let the pull of nature rule you.”
You have a right to your work, but not to its fruits.
Do not work for rewards, and do not sit and do nothing.
Work with a steady mind, because skill in work is a kind of yoga.
A wise person leaves doubt behind and finds a calm and settled mind.
Arjuna asked, “How does a wise person talk, sit and walk?”
The wise person gives up all wishes and is happy in the self.
The wise are not shaken by sorrow, and they have no fear or anger.
A tortoise pulls in its legs, and the wise pull their senses in.
Even when you turn away from pleasures, the wish for them stays for a while.
Wild senses can pull even a wise mind away, so hold them.
If you keep thinking about something, you start to want it more.
Wanting leads to anger, anger leads to confusion, and confusion ruins the mind.
A person who is free from like and dislike finds a calm heart.
A mind without discipline has no peace, and without peace there is no joy.
A strong wind can push a ship away, and wild senses can push the mind.
The night of other people is the day of the wise person.
Rivers run into the sea, and the sea stays calm and still.
The person who lets go of every wish finds true peace.
Even at the end of life, a person in this state is free.
Arjuna asked, “If knowledge is better than action, why must I fight?”
Krishna said there are two paths, one of knowledge and one of work.
No one can stay without acting, even for one moment.
Work done as a gift to others keeps the whole world turning.
Great kings did their duty, and ordinary people followed their example.
Krishna said he has nothing to gain, but still he works.
Wise people work without clinging, and they are kind to those who do not understand.
It is better to do your own duty badly than another's well.
Arjuna asked what pushes a person to do wrong against his will.
Desire covers wisdom like smoke covers a fire.
Krishna said, “I taught this old knowledge to the sun long ago.”
Arjuna asked how that was possible, and Krishna said he remembers many lives.
When good ways fade, Krishna comes back to protect the good.
People come to Krishna in many ways, and he welcomes them all.
Some people want quick success, but Krishna's actions never touch him.
The wise see quiet in action, and they see action in quiet.
The wise do their work, and they are happy with what comes.
There are many ways to give, but giving knowledge is the best.
Knowledge is like a boat that carries you across the river.
Krishna said, “Cut your doubt with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.”
Arjuna asked which is better, giving up action or doing it.
A person who truly gives up the world has no hate and no wanting inside.
The wise person says, “I do nothing,” while he sees, hears and walks.
Water rolls off a lotus leaf, and wrong does not stick to a wise person.
The self lives in the body like a king in a city with nine gates.
The wise look at everyone with the same kind eye.
The wise person is not carried away by pleasure or by pain.
The person who finds joy inside is calm, and the whole world is a friend.
Do your work without hope for its fruit, and your mind will be free.
Lift yourself up by your own effort, for you are your own friend or enemy.
A seeker should sit alone in a quiet, clean place.
The yogi sits straight and still, and he thinks of Krishna.
A seeker should not eat too much or too little.
A calm mind is like a lamp that does not flicker in still air.
The yogi finds a joy that is deeper than any pleasure.
When the mind runs away, bring it back again, gently.
The best yogi sees himself in everyone, and everyone in himself.
Arjuna said the mind is as wild as the wind.
Krishna said that no good effort is ever wasted.
After many lives, a person who keeps trying reaches the highest goal.
Krishna said that few people search for him, and fewer still know him.
Krishna said the whole world is held on him like pearls on a thread.
Krishna said he is the taste in water and the light of the moon.
The world is a great illusion, but those who trust Krishna can cross it.
People come to Krishna in trouble, in search of knowledge, or in love.
Some people pray to many powers, but only a few find the truth.
Arjuna asked seven deep questions, and Krishna began to answer them.
The thought you hold at the end of your life leads you onward.
Worlds rise and fall like day and night, but something stays forever.
There are two paths, one of light and one of dark.
Krishna said, “Now I will tell you my royal secret.”
The whole world rests in Krishna, as the wind rests in the sky.
Everything returns to Krishna, and he sends it out again.
Foolish people do not see Krishna when he comes as a man.
Krishna said that he is the offering, the father, the mother and the friend.
Krishna looks after the people who think only of him.
A leaf, a flower or water, given with love, pleases Krishna.
Whatever you do, eat or give, do it as a gift.
Krishna is the same to all, and even the worst person can change.
People of every kind can reach the highest goal.
Krishna said that even the great sages do not know where he came from.
All good and bad feelings in the world come from Krishna.
People who love Krishna talk about him together and are happy.
Arjuna bowed and asked Krishna to tell him about his glory.
Krishna said, “I am the self that lives in every heart.”
Among lights he is the sun, and among mountains he is Meru.
Among trees he is the banyan, and among rivers he is the Ganges.
Among seasons he is spring, and he is the courage of the brave.
Among sages he is Vyasa, and among secrets he is silence.
One small part of Krishna holds up the whole world.
Arjuna said, “My doubts are gone, so please show me your true form.”
Krishna said Arjuna's eyes were too weak, so he gave him new sight.
Arjuna saw a light as bright as a thousand suns.
Arjuna saw all the gods and all the worlds inside Krishna.
Krishna had no beginning, middle or end, and Arjuna shook with wonder.
Arjuna lost his courage and begged Krishna to be kind.
The warriors rushed into Krishna like rivers into the sea.
Krishna said, “I am Time, and all these men are already finished.”
Arjuna asked Krishna to forgive him and to show his gentle face again.
Krishna smiled kindly and showed his gentle human face once more.
Arjuna was calm again and said, “Now I am myself.”
Krishna said that love and deep devotion, not study, lead to him.
Arjuna asked which is better, loving Krishna or praying to what has no shape.
Krishna lifts those who love him out of the sea of birth and death.
If you cannot do one thing, do the next, and keep going.
The one Krishna loves hates no one, forgives all and is kind.
The body is a field, and the one who knows it is the knower.
Our senses, thoughts and feelings are all part of the field.
True knowledge means being humble, patient, honest and kind.
The highest truth is the light inside every heart.
Nature does the work, but the spirit inside only watches.
People find the truth by many paths, and all are walking to one goal.
One sun lights the whole world, and the self lights the whole body.
Krishna said all beings are born from a great womb that he fills.
Nature has three strands: one is calm, one is restless, and one is dull.
Each strand wins by pushing down the others.
The wise person is the same in praise and blame.
The world is like a tree with its roots in the sky.
The self takes the mind and senses to a new body like wind takes scent.
Krishna said the light of the sun and the moon is his.
Krishna named good qualities: no fear, honesty, kindness, patience and a clean heart.
Pride, anger and harsh words lead to trouble, but good qualities set us free.
Some people think only of money and say that nobody is as great as they are.
Desire, anger and greed are three doors to trouble.
Krishna said that people have different kinds of faith, as their natures are different.
Hurting your own body out of pride is not wise.
Krishna said some food is light, some is too hot and some is stale.
A gift of work without hope of reward is the best.
Speak the truth, speak kindly, and keep your mind calm.
The best gift is given quietly, without hoping for anything back.
Arjuna asked about giving up, and Krishna said to give up the fruit.
Giving, sacrifice and discipline make wise people pure, so do not stop them.
Doing your duty without clinging to the result is the best way.
There are five causes for every action, not only the doer.
Some people see one truth in all, and some see only parts.
Action and the doer can be calm, restless or dull.
A wise mind knows what to do and what to avoid.
Some happiness is bitter first and sweet later.
Each person has duties that fit his own nature.
Do your own duty well, even if it is not perfect.
A person who lets go of desire and ego reaches the highest peace.
A peaceful person does not grieve, wants nothing and sees everyone the same.
Krishna said, “Give your work to me, and listen with care.”
Krishna said Arjuna's own nature would call him to do his duty.
Krishna said, “Think about all this, and then do as you wish.”
Krishna said, “Let go of everything else, and come to me.”
Those who teach, study or hear this book with faith are blessed.
Arjuna said, “My doubts are gone, and I will do as you say.”
Sanjaya said the talk was wonderful and filled him with joy.
Where Krishna and Arjuna stand, there will be good fortune.
B1B2: The Bhagavad Gita is a holy book of Hinduism, made of 700 verses in 18 chapters. Its name means the Song of the Lord, and it records a conversation between a prince named Arjuna and his friend Krishna.

The Gita is one small part of the Mahabharata, a huge epic poem of ancient India that tradition links to the sage Vyasa. That poem tells how two sets of cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, came to quarrel over who should rule their kingdom.

The Gita opens on a battlefield called Kurukshetra, where both armies stand ready for war. Far away, the blind king Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas, asks his minister Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas are doing there.
Sanjaya has been given a gift by Vyasa, which lets him see and hear everything on the battlefield from far away. Everything we read in the Gita is told to us through his words.
Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, sees the Pandava army standing in perfect order. He goes to his old teacher Drona and points out that it has been arranged by Drona's own clever pupil.
Duryodhana then names the greatest warriors of his own side, one by one, and says that his army is led by Bhishma. He orders every commander to stay at his post and to protect Bhishma above all.
Bhishma is the oldest and most respected man in the family. To cheer Duryodhana, he roars like a lion and blows his great conch shell, and the sound lifts the hearts of the Kaurava soldiers.
At once, shells, big drums, small drums and horns all begin to sound together in the Kaurava army. The noise grows so loud that it seems to shake the whole plain.
On the other side, Krishna and Arjuna stand in a splendid chariot pulled by white horses. Krishna blows his divine conch, called Panchajanya, and Arjuna answers with his own, called Devadatta.
Then the other Pandava brothers blow their conches as well, each one with his own name. The roar rings through earth and sky, and it shakes the hearts of the sons of Dhritarashtra.

Arjuna stands in his chariot, flying the banner of the monkey hero Hanuman, and lifts his bow as the fighting is about to start. Then he asks Krishna to stop the chariot in the space between the two armies.
Krishna drives the white horses to the middle of the field, right in front of Bhishma, Drona and all the kings. He says quietly to Arjuna, “Look, here are all the Kurus gathered together.”

Arjuna looks closely at the men who stand ready to fight, and he sees his own family there. There are fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and friends, and they stand on both sides of the field.
A deep pity comes over Arjuna, and he speaks sadly to Krishna. He says that his limbs are failing, his mouth is dry, his body is shaking and his hair is standing on end.
His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and his skin feels as if it is burning. He cannot stand, his mind seems to be spinning, and he sees only bad signs around him.

Arjuna says he can see nothing good in killing his own family in battle. He does not want victory, a kingdom or any pleasures, because the people for whom he wanted them are standing here ready to die.

Arjuna says he would not kill them even to rule the three worlds, so he certainly would not do it for the earth alone. What joy could there be in killing the sons of Dhritarashtra, he asks, when it would only bring sin and sorrow?

Arjuna adds that greedy men may not see the harm in destroying a family, but he can see it clearly. When a family is destroyed, he says, its old customs and duties die with it, and the people who remain fall into confusion.
He says sadly that they have decided to do a terrible wrong, and all because they long for the pleasures of a kingdom. It seems to him that this greed has made them ready to kill their own people.

Arjuna says it would be better for him if the armed sons of Dhritarashtra killed him while he stood there without a weapon. Having spoken, he throws down his bow and arrows and sits down on the floor of the chariot, overwhelmed by sorrow.
Krishna sees the tears in Arjuna's eyes and asks him where this weakness has come from at such a moment. It does not suit a man of his courage, he says, so Arjuna should shake it off and stand up.
Arjuna answers that he cannot imagine shooting arrows in battle at Bhishma and Drona. These two men have always deserved his respect and honour, and he cannot make them his targets.
Arjuna says it would be better to live by begging than to kill his noble teachers. Even if he won wealth and power, he would enjoy them only as things stained with the blood of those he loved.

Arjuna admits that he does not know which would be worse, to win or to lose the war. If he kills the Kauravas, he says, he would no longer wish to live himself, and yet they are the ones who stand before him.

Arjuna says that his mind is confused about what is right, and that he has been struck by a weakness that he cannot understand. He asks Krishna to tell him clearly what is best, and he says, “I am your student, so please teach me.”
Arjuna says he cannot see anything that would take away the grief that dries up his senses. Even a rich kingdom on earth, or lordship over the gods in heaven, would not help him.
Arjuna tells Krishna, “I will not fight,” and then he becomes silent. Time seems to stand still in that moment between the two great armies.
Between the two armies, Krishna turns to the sad prince, and as if with a smile he begins to speak. These are the first words of his teaching, and they come gently, without anger.
Krishna tells Arjuna that he is grieving for people who should not be grieved for, and yet he speaks like a wise man. The truly wise, Krishna says, grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.

Krishna says that he, Arjuna and all these kings have always existed and will never cease to be. In this body the self passes through childhood, youth and old age, and in the same way it passes into another body.

Krishna begins by telling Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain, are felt through the senses and pass like the seasons. He should bear them calmly, because whoever is not shaken by them is ready for freedom.
The unreal, Krishna says, has no lasting being, while the real never ceases to exist. The wise have seen this truth, and they know that what fills the whole world cannot be destroyed by anyone.

Bodies, says Krishna, have an end, but the one who lives in the body is eternal and cannot be destroyed. So the one who thinks he kills and the one who thinks he is killed are both wrong, for the self neither kills nor dies.
Krishna says that the self is never born and never dies, and that it did not come into being and will not stop being. It is unborn, eternal and ancient, and it is not killed when the body is killed.
No weapon can cut the self, Krishna explains, and fire cannot burn it. Water cannot make it wet, and wind cannot dry it, for it stays the same through everything.
Krishna gives a simple picture to make the idea clear. Just as a person throws away worn clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves old bodies and takes new ones.
The self cannot be seen with the eyes, and it cannot be fully grasped by thought. It does not change, says Krishna, and when Arjuna understands this, he should not grieve.

Krishna then offers another thought, in case Arjuna still believes the self is born and dies again and again. Even so, death is certain for everyone who is born and birth is certain for the dead, so there is nothing to grieve over.
Krishna says that beings are unseen before birth, seen for a short time in the middle, and unseen again after death. Since this is the way of everything, he asks, why should anyone weep?

Krishna says that some people see the self as a wonder, others speak of it as one, and others hear of it as one. Even so, no one fully understands it, and the one who lives in every body can never be killed.
Krishna reminds Arjuna to think of his own duty and not to tremble. A warrior has nothing better than a fair fight, and one who finds it unsought is lucky, for it opens a door to heaven.
If Arjuna refuses to fight this lawful battle, Krishna says, he will give up his duty and his good name. In that case he will have brought harm upon himself instead of keeping his honour.
People will speak of his disgrace for years to come. For a man who has been honoured all his life, Krishna says, shame is worse than death.

The great warriors will believe that Arjuna left the field because of fear, and those who once respected him will think little of him. His enemies will say many cruel things about his strength, and nothing could hurt him more than that.
Krishna says that if Arjuna is killed he will reach heaven, and if he wins he will enjoy the earth. So he should rise, make up his mind and fight.
Krishna tells him to look on pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat as the same. If he fights with this even mind, then no sin will touch him.

Krishna says that he has explained the wisdom of understanding the self, and now he will explain the wisdom of right action. Holding to it, Arjuna will break free from the chains that action usually brings.
On this path, Krishna says, no effort is ever wasted and no harm is done. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear.
Krishna says that the mind of a person who has decided is single and firm. The minds of those who have not decided have many branches and go off in endless directions.
Krishna says that some people with little understanding are fond of flowery words. They long for heaven, pleasure and power, and so their minds can never rest in a firm decision.

Krishna tells Arjuna that people are pulled in different ways by the three strands of nature. He should rise above them and above the pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain, and stay steady in the self.
Then Krishna gives one of the best-known teachings in the whole poem. You have a right to your actions, he says, but never to the fruits of your actions.

Krishna says that Arjuna must not let the results be his reason for acting, and he must not become attached to doing nothing either. He should act with an even mind, giving up attachment and treating success and failure alike.
Action done for a reward, Krishna says, is far lower than action done with a steady mind. He tells Arjuna to take refuge in that steady wisdom, and he says that yoga is skill in action.

The wise, Krishna says, give up the fruits of their actions and are freed from the cycle of birth. When Arjuna's mind has crossed the thicket of confusion, he will find peace even when he hears many opinions.
Arjuna listens closely, and then he asks the question that has been on his mind. What are the signs of a person of steady wisdom, he wants to know, and how does that person speak, sit and walk?
Krishna answers that the steady person has given up all the desires of the mind and is content in the self alone. Such a person has no need of anything outside, because peace is found within.
This person is not shaken by sorrow and does not crave pleasure. Fear, passion and anger have faded from him, and he neither rejoices at good luck nor hates bad luck.
Krishna gives a famous picture to show what the steady mind is like. Just as a tortoise draws its limbs inside its shell, the wise person draws the senses back from their objects.
Krishna admits that a person can turn away from sense objects and still keep the taste for them. That taste, he says, only fades completely when the person has seen something higher.
Krishna says that the senses are so strong and restless that they can carry off the mind of even a wise person. So Arjuna must hold them all in check and keep his mind fixed on the highest.
Here Krishna describes how trouble begins in the mind. When a person keeps dwelling on the objects of the senses, attachment grows, then desire is born, and from desire comes anger.
Krishna goes on to show how anger leads to confusion, and confusion to a loss of memory. When memory is lost, reason is destroyed, and when reason is destroyed, the person is ruined.

A person who moves among the objects of the senses, free of liking and disliking, finds a peaceful clearness of mind. In that peace, Krishna says, all sorrow comes to an end, and the mind becomes steady.
Krishna says that a person without discipline cannot have steady wisdom and cannot meditate, and a person who cannot meditate has no peace. Without peace, he asks, how can there be any happiness?
Krishna compares the mind to a ship on the sea. When a wandering sense takes hold of the mind, it carries away wisdom as the wind carries a boat from its course.

The one whose senses are held back from their objects has steady wisdom, Krishna says. What is night for most people is wakefulness for the self-controlled, and what others call waking is like night to a sage who sees.
Krishna gives a picture of what true peace is like. The ocean is filled by rivers and yet stays calm, so whoever is not disturbed by desires finds peace.

The person who has given up every longing, and who moves through life without any sense of ownership or ego, attains peace. He no longer holds on to the things he has, and so there is nothing to lose.
Krishna says that this is the state of union with Brahman, the highest reality. Once a person reaches it he is never again deluded, and even at the end of life he is freed.
Arjuna is puzzled, and he tells Krishna that if knowledge is higher than action, he does not see why he must do this terrible deed. These mixed words, he says, seem to confuse his mind.

Krishna explains that there are two paths, the path of knowledge for those who reflect and the path of action for those who work. Nobody reaches freedom by simply refusing to act, he says, and no one reaches perfection just by giving up the world.

Nobody can remain without acting even for a single moment, Krishna says, because nature itself drives every being to act. A person who holds back his body but keeps thinking about pleasures only fools himself, and the better one controls his senses and works.

Krishna says that work done as an offering, and not for oneself, keeps the world in motion. Everything is a wheel of giving and receiving, he says, and the one who only takes and never gives is a kind of thief.
Krishna points out that King Janaka and others reached perfection through action alone. Whatever a great person does, other people copy, so a leader sets the standard that the world follows.

Krishna says that he himself has no duty in the three worlds and nothing left to gain. Yet he keeps working, because if he stopped, everyone would follow his example, and the world would fall into ruin.

Krishna says that those who do not understand act out of attachment, but the wise act without attachment for the good of the world. The wise must not shake the minds of the ignorant, but should show them by example how to do their work well.

Krishna says that even a wise person acts according to his own nature, and nature cannot be forced. It is better to do your own duty imperfectly than another person's duty well, he says, because following another's path is full of danger.

Arjuna asks what drives a person to do wrong even when he does not wish to, as if some force were pushing him. Krishna answers that it is desire, and anger born of desire, and that these are the great enemies.

Krishna says that as smoke covers fire and dust covers a mirror, so desire covers wisdom. He tells Arjuna to rule the senses first, because they are the home of desire, and then to use mind and intellect.

Krishna says that long ago he taught this ancient teaching to Vivasvan, the sun god, who passed it on to Manu. It was handed down through royal teachers, but over time it was lost, so now he teaches it to Arjuna, his friend and devotee.

Arjuna is surprised, because Vivasvan lived long before Krishna was born, and he asks how this could be. Krishna replies that both of them have lived through many births, and that he remembers them all while Arjuna does not.

Krishna says that although he is unborn and does not change, he takes a body by using his own power. Whenever righteousness declines and wrong grows strong, he comes into the world to protect the good, to stop the wicked and to restore dharma.

One who truly understands Krishna's divine birth and work is not born again, and many have been purified by knowledge and have reached him. However people approach him, he welcomes them in the same way, for all paths lead to him.

Krishna says that people who want quick success from their actions worship the powers of nature. His own actions never touch him, because he has no desire for their fruits, and the wise of ancient times acted as he does.
Even the wise, Krishna admits, are confused about what action is and what inaction is. The one who sees inaction in the middle of action, and action in the middle of inaction, he says, is truly wise.
Krishna describes the wise person in a few calm words. Such a person wants nothing from his work and is free from envy, so he is never bound, even while he acts.
Krishna lists many kinds of sacrifice, from giving wealth to practising discipline, studying or controlling the breath. He says that the sacrifice of knowledge is better than the sacrifice of things.

Krishna tells Arjuna to find wise teachers and to ask them questions humbly, for those who have seen the truth will teach it. He says that even the worst of sinners can cross over all evil in the boat of knowledge.

As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, Krishna says, the fire of knowledge burns up the bonds of action. So Arjuna must take the sword of knowledge, cut the doubt in his heart and stand up, ready to act.
Arjuna says that Krishna praises giving up action and also praises doing it, so which is better? Krishna answers that both lead to the highest, but that the path of action is better.

Krishna says that the true renouncer is the one who neither hates nor desires anything. Only children, he adds, think that knowledge and action are different paths, since the person who follows either one well reaches the same goal.

The one who knows the truth thinks, I do nothing at all, even while seeing, hearing, touching, eating, walking and breathing. He understands that the senses are only moving among their objects, and so he is not carried away by his own deeds.
A person who acts by offering his actions to the highest, and who gives up attachment, is not touched by wrong. He is like a lotus leaf, which stays dry although it floats on water.

Krishna says that the self rests happily in the body, like a king in a city with nine gates, neither acting nor making others act. Ignorance covers wisdom, but knowledge destroys it and shines like the sun, showing what is highest.
Krishna says that wise people look with an equal eye on a learned and humble scholar, a cow, an elephant and a dog. Even in this life, those whose minds rest in equality have conquered the world.

The person who is not excited by pleasure or upset by pain stays steady and clear. Pleasure from the senses has a beginning and an end, so the wise seek joy elsewhere, and those who master desire and anger are happy.

Such a person finds joy and light inside himself, and he reaches a peace that is free from sin and doubt. Krishna says that those who know him as the friend of all beings, and the Lord of all the worlds, attain peace.

The true renouncer, Krishna says, is not the person who gives up work but the one who works without depending on the results. For the beginner, action is the way upward, while for the one who has already climbed, stillness becomes the way.

Krishna says that Arjuna must lift himself up and not let himself sink, for the self is its own friend and also its own enemy. The yogi who has conquered the mind sees a lump of clay, a stone and gold as the same, and treats friends and enemies alike.
Krishna describes how a yogi should practise in a quiet place. He should live alone and sit on a firm seat that is neither too high nor too low, keeping his mind steady on one point.
The yogi sits with his body, head and neck straight and still, and he does not look around restlessly. Calm and fearless, with his mind under control, he thinks of Krishna and so finds peace.

Krishna warns that yoga is not for the person who eats too much or fasts too much, or who sleeps too much or too little. For the one who is moderate in food, play, work, sleep and waking, yoga puts an end to sorrow.
When the mind is controlled and rests in the self alone, free from every craving, the yogi is called steady. Krishna compares this to a lamp in a place without wind, which does not flicker.
When the mind finds rest in this way, the yogi sees the self by the self and is happy. He finds a joy that the senses cannot give, and once he has found it he is not shaken even by great sorrow.

Krishna tells Arjuna to give up desires born of imagination and to quiet the senses by the power of the mind. Wherever the restless mind wanders, he says, the yogi should bring it back gently and keep it under the control of the self.
The best yogi, Krishna says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. He sees Krishna everywhere, and he feels the joy and pain of every living thing as if they were his own.

Arjuna says that the mind is restless, strong and stubborn, and that holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. Krishna agrees that it is hard to control, but he says it can be held by regular practice and by detachment.
Arjuna asks whether a sincere seeker who fails is lost like a broken cloud, with no support on either path. Krishna says that no good effort is ever wasted.

Krishna says that the sincere seeker is born again in a good family, where he can begin from what he learned before. By striving through many births he reaches the highest goal, so Krishna tells Arjuna to be a yogi.

Krishna promises to teach Arjuna the knowledge that comes with real experience. Among thousands of people, he says, only one strives for perfection, and among those who strive, hardly one knows him as he truly is.
