Krishna says his nature has eight parts: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego. Beyond these is a higher nature that gives life to the world, and everything is strung on him like pearls on a thread.
Krishna says he is the taste in water and the light of the moon and sun. He is also the sacred sound Om, the pure fragrance of earth and the life in all living beings.
The three strands of nature come from Krishna, but he is not bound by them. This divine illusion is hard to cross, he says, but those who take refuge in him cross it easily.

Four kinds of good people worship Krishna: the person in trouble, the one who seeks knowledge, the one who seeks wealth, and the wise. The wise person, who is steady and loves only him, is the dearest of all, and such a great soul is very rare.

Krishna says that those who worship other powers do so because of their desires, and that he steadies their faith. The rewards they receive are small and do not last, and he is hidden from most of the world by his divine power.

Arjuna now asks seven questions at once, about Brahman, the self, action, the nature of the world and what happens at the moment of death. Krishna answers that Brahman is the imperishable highest reality, and that he himself is the lord of sacrifice in the body.

Krishna says that whatever a person remembers at the end of life, that is what he reaches. So Arjuna should remember him at all times and still fight, for his mind and intellect will then belong to Krishna.

Krishna describes how worlds come and go in great cycles, like a day and night of the creator Brahma. Beyond them, he says, there is another eternal existence that does not perish when everything else does, and those who reach it do not return.
Krishna speaks of two paths by which yogis leave this world, one of light and one of darkness. One leads to a return and the other does not, and the yogi who knows both is not confused.

Krishna says he will now tell Arjuna the royal secret, a knowledge that can be seen directly and is the greatest of all purifiers. It is joyful to practise and it never fades, but people without faith do not reach it.
Krishna says that the whole world is filled by him, though he cannot be seen. All beings rest in him, as the mighty wind rests in the sky, yet he is not tied to any of them.

At the end of an age, Krishna says, all beings return to his nature, and in the next age he sends them out again. These acts do not bind him, because he sits like a witness who is not attached to what he sees.

Fools do not recognise Krishna when he lives in a human form, because they do not know his higher nature. Great souls, however, know that he is the source of all, and they worship him with undivided minds.
Krishna says that he is the ritual, the offering, the father, the mother and the support of the world. He is the friend, the refuge and the goal, and he is also the heat of the sun and the rain.

Those who follow rituals only for rewards enjoy heaven for a time, but they return to the earth when their merit is used up. To those who think only of him, Krishna says, he brings whatever they lack and protects whatever they have.
Krishna says, “If someone offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, I accept it.” What matters to him is the devotion of a pure heart, and not the size or the price of the gift.

Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever he does, eats, offers or gives, or whatever discipline he practises, he should do it as an offering. In this way he will be freed from the bonds of good and bad results and will come to Krishna.

Krishna says that he is the same to all beings, and none is hateful or dear to him. Even the worst sinner who turns to him with full devotion should be called righteous, and he soon finds lasting peace.

Krishna says that even those whom society looks down on can reach the highest goal if they take refuge in him. He tells Arjuna to fix his mind on him, be devoted and bow to him, and then he will surely come to him.
Krishna tells Arjuna that he will give him a supreme teaching for his good. Neither the gods nor the great sages know his origin, he says, because he is the source of them all.
All the qualities of living beings, Krishna says, come from him alone. Wisdom and forgiveness, truth and calm, pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness are all born from him.

Krishna says that those who understand his glory fix their minds on him and give their lives to him. They talk about him together and are content, and out of kindness he lights in their hearts the lamp of knowledge, which destroys ignorance.

Arjuna is moved, and he praises Krishna as the supreme Brahman and the highest home, as sages like Narada and Vyasa have said. He asks Krishna to describe his divine glories, because he cannot hear enough of his words.
Krishna agrees to tell Arjuna about his chief glories, since there is no end to them. First, he says, he is the self in the heart of every being, and also the beginning, middle and end of all things.
Krishna names the finest of each kind of thing in the world, one after another. Among lights he is the sun, among stars the moon, among mountains the great Meru, and among waters the ocean.
Among trees, Krishna says, he is the banyan, and among beasts he is the lion. Among rivers he is the Ganges, among purifiers he is the wind, and among men he is the king.
Among seasons, Krishna says, he is the spring, and among letters he is the first. He is also the splendour of the splendid, the courage of the brave, victory, effort and the goodness of the good.
Among the Pandavas, Krishna says, he is Arjuna, and among the sages he is Vyasa. He is also silence among secrets, and wisdom among the wise.

Krishna says he is the seed of every living thing, and nothing could exist without him. There is no end to his glories, and what he has named is only a sample, for one fragment of himself holds up the universe.

Arjuna tells Krishna that his confusion has gone, because he has heard in detail about the origin and end of all beings. Now he asks to see Krishna's divine form, if Krishna thinks that he is able to see it.
Krishna tells Arjuna to look at his forms by the hundreds and the thousands, of many kinds, colours and shapes. He says Arjuna cannot see them with his own eyes, so he gives him a divine eye.

Sanjaya tells the blind king that Krishna then showed his supreme form, with many mouths, eyes and raised weapons. If the light of a thousand suns rose in the sky at once, he says, it might resemble that great radiance.

Arjuna sees the whole universe in one place inside Krishna's body, with all the gods, the sages and all kinds of beings. He is amazed, his hair stands on end, and he sees that this form has no beginning, middle or end.

Arjuna sees Krishna with endless arms, and with the sun and the moon as his eyes, touching the sky and filling every direction. The three worlds tremble before this form, and Arjuna himself shakes with fear.
Arjuna sees the great blazing mouths and loses his sense of direction, and he can find neither courage nor peace. He begs Krishna to be merciful, because his heart is shaking.
Arjuna sees the great warriors of both armies rushing into the blazing mouths, like rivers flowing into the sea or moths into a flame. In fear, he asks who Krishna is in this terrible form.

Krishna answers that he is Time, the great destroyer of the worlds, and that he has come to end them. Even without Arjuna, he says, these warriors are already slain by him, so Arjuna should rise and be merely his instrument.

Arjuna bows and speaks in a trembling voice, praising Krishna as the original god and the refuge of the universe. He asks forgiveness for calling Krishna a mere friend, as a son asks a father, and begs to see his gentle form again.

Krishna says that he has shown this form by his own power and favour, and that no one except Arjuna has ever seen it. Then he tells Arjuna not to be afraid, and, becoming gentle again, he shows his human form and comforts him.

Seeing Krishna's gentle human form again, Arjuna says that his mind is calm and he is himself again. Krishna replies that this great form is very hard to see, and that even the gods always long to see it.
Krishna says that no study, gift, ritual or hard discipline can win this vision. Only single-minded devotion can, and the one who works for Krishna, free from hatred and attachment, will come to him.

Arjuna asks which are better yogis, those who always worship Krishna with devotion or those who worship the imperishable and unseen. Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him with supreme faith are best.

Krishna says that those who worship the formless also reach him, but the path is harder for people who live in a body. As for those who devote all actions to him, he says he quickly lifts them from the ocean of birth and death.
Krishna gives steps for every ability, saying that if you cannot fix your mind on him, you can practise, or work for him. If even that is hard, you can at least give up the fruits of your actions.
The devotee who is dear to Krishna hates no being and is friendly, kind and free from ego. He is steady in pleasure and pain, forgiving, content, and equal in praise and blame.
The chapter begins with a simple picture, as Krishna tells Arjuna that the body is called the field. The one who knows it, he says, is the knower of the field.
Krishna lists what the field contains: the great elements, the ego, the intellect, the senses, the mind and its objects. It also holds desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, and the will, which all change.
Krishna explains that true knowledge is made of humility, harmlessness, patience and honesty. It also includes serving the teacher, purity, self-control and unswerving devotion to him.
Krishna says that the highest reality has no beginning, and that it is neither near nor far. It is the light of all lights, beyond darkness, and it sits in the heart of everyone.
Krishna says that nature and the spirit both have no beginning. Nature does the acting, while the spirit within the body is the witness who permits, supports and experiences.

Krishna says that some people find the self through meditation, some through knowledge, some through action, and some by hearing from others and having faith. The one who sees the Lord living equally in all beings does not harm himself by harming others.

One who sees that all actions are done by nature, and that the self is not the doer, truly sees. Space is too subtle to be stained, and so is the self, and as one sun lights the world, the knower lights the field.

Krishna announces that he will teach the supreme knowledge, by which the sages have reached perfection. The great Brahman is his womb, he says, and in it he places the seed from which all beings are born.
Krishna explains that nature has three strands, called sattva, rajas and tamas. Bright sattva, restless rajas and dull tamas each bind a person in a different way.
Krishna says that each strand rises by overcoming the other two. Sattva leads upward, rajas leaves a person in the middle, and tamas drags him downward.

One who sees beyond the three strands, Krishna says, is the same in pleasure and pain, in praise and blame, and in gold and clay. Such a person crosses beyond the strands by devotion, and reaches the home of immortality.

Krishna describes the world as a great tree with its roots above and its branches below, and its leaves are hymns. It must be cut with the strong axe of detachment, he says, and then Arjuna should seek the place from which no one returns.
Krishna says that a small part of himself becomes the living self in each being. When it leaves one body for another, it takes the mind and senses along, as the wind carries scent from a flower.

Krishna says that the light in the sun, the moon and fire is his, and that he sits in the heart of every being. He is higher than the perishable and the imperishable, so he is called the highest person.

Krishna lists the divine qualities, and the list is long and gentle. It includes fearlessness, purity of heart, charity, self-control, truth, freedom from anger, compassion, gentleness, forgiveness and freedom from pride.

Krishna says that hypocrisy, arrogance, anger and harshness belong to the ungodly nature. Divine qualities lead to freedom and ungodly ones to bondage, and he tells Arjuna not to grieve, because he was born with divine qualities.

Krishna describes people who think only of wealth and pleasure and who are never satisfied. They boast that they are rich and powerful and that no one is their equal, and so they fall deeper into confusion.
Krishna says that desire, anger and greed are three gates to ruin. A wise person gives them up, and so Arjuna should let the scriptures guide what he does and what he avoids.

Arjuna asks about those who have faith but do not follow the rules of the scriptures. Krishna answers that faith is of three kinds, following a person's nature, and that a person is made of his faith.

Krishna says that people worship in different ways, according to their natures. Those who torture their bodies with harsh discipline out of pride and ego are mistaken, because they also trouble the divine presence within.
Krishna describes three kinds of food that people like. Some is light and nourishing and brings health and joy, some is bitter, hot and harsh, and some is stale and tasteless.
Krishna says that a sacrifice offered as a duty, without desire for reward, is the best kind. One offered for show or for a reward is lower, and one done without faith or care is lowest.

Krishna says that discipline of the body means respect for teachers, purity and non-violence. Discipline of speech is words that are truthful, pleasant and helpful, and discipline of the mind is calm, gentleness and a pure heart.

The best gift, Krishna says, is given as a duty, at the right time and place, to someone who cannot repay it. Acts done with faith are marked by the sacred words Om Tat Sat, but without faith, even great acts are worth nothing.

Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the truth of renunciation and relinquishment, and how they differ. Krishna says that wise people call giving up actions done from desire renunciation, and giving up the fruits of every action relinquishment.
Krishna says that acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline should never be given up, because they purify the wise. But they should be done without attachment and without desire for their fruits.

Giving up one's duty out of confusion is poor renunciation, and so is giving it up because the effort is painful. The best kind is to do one's duty because it must be done, giving up attachment, since no embodied being can give up all action.
Krishna names five causes of any action: the body, the doer, the senses, the many kinds of effort and, fifth, destiny. A person who thinks that the self alone is the doer does not see rightly.

Krishna says that knowledge is of three kinds, and the best sees one imperishable reality in all beings. Another kind sees many separate things, and the lowest clings to one small thing as if it were the whole.
Krishna describes action and the doer in the same way, in three kinds. The best action is done as a duty without attachment, the middling with ego and strain, and the worst in confusion.
Intellect and steadiness are also of three kinds, Krishna says. The best intellect knows what ought to be done, what to fear and what not to fear, and what sets a person free.

Krishna says that the highest happiness is like poison at first and nectar at the end, because it is born of a calm mind. Happiness from the senses is the reverse, sweet at first and bitter at the end, and the lowest kind is dull from beginning to end.
Krishna says that no being on earth is free from the three strands of nature. In the language of its time, he says that people form four groups, each with duties that suit its nature.

Krishna says that each person reaches perfection by honouring the divine through his own work. It is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than another's well, since every task has some fault, as every fire has smoke.

Krishna describes the person whose mind is free from attachment and who wants nothing. Living simply, he meditates daily and lets go of ego, pride and anger, so he is ready to become one with Brahman.

Having become one with Brahman, the person is serene, neither grieving nor craving anything. He sees all beings as the same, and by devotion he comes to know Krishna as he truly is and then enters into him.

Krishna says that even a person busy with all kinds of actions reaches the eternal home by his grace, if he takes refuge in him. So Arjuna should surrender all his actions to Krishna and fix his mind on him, and then he will overcome every obstacle.
Krishna warns that if Arjuna refuses to fight out of ego, his decision will be useless. His own nature will compel him to act, since the Lord lives in the hearts of all beings.

Krishna tells Arjuna to take refuge in him alone, with his whole being, and he will reach supreme peace by his grace. Krishna has now told him the most secret knowledge, so Arjuna should think it over fully and then do as he wishes.
Krishna gives his supreme word, the most secret of all, because Arjuna is dear to him. Let go of every other support and take refuge in me alone, he says, and I will free you, so do not grieve.

Krishna says that this teaching should not be shared with those who do not want to hear it or who speak ill of him. Those who teach it to his devotees, who study it or who listen with faith and without envy are blessed.

Krishna asks Arjuna whether he has listened with a single mind, and whether his confusion born of ignorance has been destroyed. Arjuna answers that his confusion is gone and his doubts are over, and that he will act according to Krishna's word.

Sanjaya tells the blind king that he has heard this wonderful conversation between Krishna and the great-souled Arjuna. By the grace of Vyasa he has heard it directly, and remembering it again and again fills him with joy.

Sanjaya says that wherever Krishna, the lord of yoga, stands with Arjuna the archer, there will be good fortune, victory and justice. The Gita ends there, before the battle begins, but its conversation about how to live has been read and loved for centuries.
C1C2: The Bhagavad Gita, whose name means the Song of the Lord, is a sacred text of Hinduism, made up of 700 verses in 18 chapters. It forms a small part of the Mahabharata, the great epic of ancient India, and takes the shape of a conversation between the prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna. For many centuries readers have turned to it as a guide to duty, devotion and the search for inner peace.

The Mahabharata, which tradition links to the sage Vyasa, is one of the longest poems ever composed, and it tells the story of a royal family torn apart. The Pandavas, five brothers led by the upright Yudhishthira, and the Kauravas, a hundred cousins led by the proud Duryodhana, quarrel for years over the throne, and every attempt at peace fails. The Gita is set on the very morning when the two armies finally face each other, at the edge of war.

The Gita opens with a question, spoken from a palace far from the fighting by the blind king Dhritarashtra, who is the father of the Kauravas. He asks his minister Sanjaya what his own sons and the Pandavas have been doing on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, now that they have gathered there to fight. The answer will take eighteen chapters, and it turns out to be about much more than one battle.

Sanjaya can answer because the sage Vyasa has given him a rare gift, the power to see and hear all that happens on the field, however far away he sits. Calmly, and without taking sides, he describes the armies, the commanders and the words spoken between them. It is through his careful reporting that every verse of the Gita reaches the blind king, and then reaches us.

Duryodhana, anxious and watchful, surveys the Pandava host drawn up in perfect order and hurries to his old teacher Drona to speak. He points out, perhaps with a trace of mockery, that this formidable army has been arranged by Drona's own gifted pupil, a man who once came to him to learn the art of war. In this way the Gita already shows us a mind full of worry hiding behind boasts.

Duryodhana then names, one after another, the great warriors who fight on his side, among them Drona himself, Bhishma, Karna and Kripa. He declares that his army is led by Bhishma, and he commands all the commanders to hold their posts firmly and to guard the old man above everything else. His words sound confident, yet they betray a leader who is more afraid than he wishes to admit.

Bhishma, the oldest and most honoured member of the family, understands what Duryodhana needs at that moment. He lets out a roar like a lion's and blows his great conch, so as to lift the courage of the prince who is trembling beside him. The deep note rolls across the plain, and it is the first sound of a war that no one has been able to prevent.

As if a signal had been given, conches, kettledrums, tabors and horns burst out together all along the Kaurava line, and the tumult is overwhelming. The din rises from thousands of throats and instruments at once, rolling over the plain like thunder trapped between the hills. For a moment it seems that nothing could be said or thought in the midst of such noise.

From the other side, in a splendid chariot drawn by white horses, Krishna and Arjuna answer the challenge. Krishna sounds his divine conch, called Panchajanya, and Arjuna sounds his own, called Devadatta, so that both rise clear and unafraid above the confusion. The tradition honours Krishna as the Lord himself in human form, and yet here he sits quietly in the humble seat of a charioteer.

Next, the other Pandavas lift their conches too, each shell carrying a name of its own: Yudhishthira the eldest brother, the mighty Bhima, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. The great roar that follows echoes through earth and sky, and the verses say that it tears the hearts of the sons of Dhritarashtra. The Kauravas have made the first noise of the day, but it is the Pandavas who make the deeper one.

Arjuna, standing tall in his chariot beneath the banner of the monkey hero Hanuman, sees the Kaurava army in battle order and raises his bow, for the first arrows are about to fly. Yet at the last moment he turns to his charioteer with a strange request. He asks Krishna to bring the chariot to a halt in the open ground between the two armies, so that he may look carefully at the men with whom he must fight.

Krishna does as he is asked, driving the white horses into the empty space that lies directly in front of Bhishma, Drona and all the kings of the earth. He speaks only a few words, in a quiet voice, telling Arjuna to look at the Kurus who have gathered there. Nothing in his tone suggests that these simple words will begin the longest and deepest conversation of the poem.

Arjuna looks along the lines, and what he sees is not an enemy but a family. Standing in front of him are his fathers and grandfathers, his teachers, his uncles and cousins, his sons and grandsons, and his friends, and they are arranged on both sides of the field. The sight is more than he can bear, because he understands that no victory will leave any of these faces untouched.

A deep compassion overwhelms the great archer, and he speaks to Krishna in a voice full of sadness. His limbs, he says, are giving way, his mouth is parched, his body is trembling and the hair on his arms is standing on end. The warrior who had feared no one until that morning now stands shaken by the thought of what he is about to do.

The mighty bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and his skin seems to burn as if with fever. He can no longer hold himself upright, his mind spins in confusion, and he tells Krishna that he sees only bad omens in the sky and on the ground. It is a vivid picture of a person who has lost all inner balance at the moment when action is demanded of him.

Arjuna cannot see what good can come from killing his own relatives in battle, and he says plainly that he wants neither victory nor a kingdom nor any pleasure. What is the use of power, or of enjoyment, or even of life itself, he asks, when the very people for whom we desire such things are standing here, ready to give them all up? His argument is simple and human, and for that reason it is difficult to answer.

He declares that he would not kill them even for the rule of the three worlds, so he would certainly not do it for the sake of one small piece of earth. He asks what lasting joy could come from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra, and he foresees only sin and sorrow clinging to the victors. His grief has begun to look less like weakness and more like a very serious moral objection to war.

Greed, Arjuna says, has clouded the minds of the Kauravas, so that they cannot see the harm in destroying their own kin; but he himself sees it plainly and cannot turn away. When a family falls, he reasons, its ancient customs and duties perish with it, and the people who are left fall into disorder that spreads from one generation to the next. Behind his words stands an old fear, the fear that a society can be ruined by the very victories it wins.

The prince cries out that they are preparing to commit a great wrong, and all for the sake of the pleasures of royal power. It horrifies him that men who know better can be driven by greed to kill their own people for the sake of a throne. In this passage the poem lets a hero doubt the cause he has been brought up to serve, and it does not hurry to condemn him.

Arjuna concludes that it would be better for him if the armed sons of Dhritarashtra struck him down while he stood there unresisting and without a weapon. With these words he casts away his bow and arrows, and he sinks down onto the seat of the chariot, his heart overcome with grief. So ends the first chapter, which the tradition calls the yoga of Arjuna's despair.

Krishna looks at the prince who only a moment before had stood proudly in his chariot and now sits with tears in his eyes. He asks where this dejection has come from, at such a moment of crisis, since it brings neither honour nor lasting good to anyone. Weakness of heart does not suit a man like Arjuna, he says, and he urges him to cast it off and to stand up.

Arjuna, still shaken, protests that he cannot possibly fight Bhishma and Drona in battle, since they are the very men to whom he owes his respect. How, he asks, could he aim his arrows at the grandfather he has loved since childhood, or at the teacher who taught him the art of archery? The question is spoken with the whole force of his love and his upbringing.

He says that it would be better to live on alms in this world than to take the lives of his noble teachers, because any wealth gained by their deaths would be soaked in blood. Even if they were driven by greed, he cannot forget that they are his elders and guides. Arjuna prefers a beggar's bowl to a throne that would rest on such a foundation.

Arjuna confesses that he does not know which result would be worse for them, victory or defeat, since in either case he would lose the people he loves. If he kills the sons of Dhritarashtra, he would not wish to live afterward, and yet they are the very men who now stand ready to fight. The poem lets a perplexed man state his dilemma in the plainest possible words.

His whole nature, he says, has been struck by a weakness that he cannot overcome, and his mind is so clouded that he cannot tell where his duty lies. Humbly, he asks Krishna to say definitely what is best for him, and he takes the posture of a pupil before a teacher, saying that he has come for refuge. This is the moment when the dialogue of the Gita truly begins, because a friend becomes a student.

Arjuna adds that he cannot see anything that would dry up the sorrow that burns his senses, not even the winning of a flourishing kingdom on earth or the lordship of the gods in heaven. All the usual prizes of a warrior's life have lost their taste for him. What he longs for now is not a reward of any kind but a true and lasting answer to his sorrow.

After saying all this to Krishna, who knows every heart, the great archer announces simply that he will not fight, and then he falls silent. A stillness descends on the little space between the two armies, while thousands of soldiers wait for a signal that does not come. It is one of the most striking pauses in all of literature, and the whole teaching of the Gita is born inside it.

In the middle of the two armies, Krishna turns to the grieving prince and, with something like a smile, begins to speak. The tradition notes this small detail, because it shows that the Lord's calm is not disturbed by the chaos around him, and it comforts the one who is suffering. What follows is a long answer to a single cry of despair, and it begins with a gentle correction.

You grieve, says Krishna, for people who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words that sound like wisdom. The truly wise, he says, do not mourn for the living, and they do not mourn for the dead either, because they see beyond the body to what lies within. With this statement he opens the central subject of the Gita, which is the question of what a human being really is.

Never was there a time, Krishna says, when he himself did not exist, nor Arjuna, nor any of these kings, and never will there be a time when we all cease to be. Just as the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, so the same one passes on to another body, and a wise person is not troubled by that. These two verses introduce the idea of the eternal self, which the next chapters will explore.

Krishna begins his teaching with a lesson about experience, telling Arjuna that the touch of the senses brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and that all of these come and go like the seasons. They do not last, he says, and so a person must learn to bear them without complaint. The one who is not disturbed by such changes, who stays steady in sorrow and in joy alike, is fit for immortality.

The unreal, according to Krishna, never has true being, while the real never ceases to be, and the seers who see the final truth have understood both of these facts. Whatever pervades this whole universe, he adds, is imperishable, and no power on earth is able to destroy it. With this single sentence the argument moves from the fear of death to a calm trust in what lies behind appearances.

The bodies of this eternal and indestructible being, Krishna says, are said to come to an end, so Arjuna should fight and not give in to sorrow. The person who thinks that he is the killer and the one who thinks that he is killed are both mistaken, because the self neither kills nor is killed. This is a startling idea to put to a soldier, for it removes neither his duty nor his responsibility, and yet it lifts the weight of fear.

The self is never born, Krishna declares, and it never dies, nor is it something that came into being once and will cease to be again. It is unborn, constant, eternal and ancient, and it is not slain when the body is slain. These words have been recited for thousands of years by people who wished to understand what survives the loss of a loved one.

Weapons cannot cut the self, Krishna says, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it and the wind cannot dry it. It is everlasting, all-pervading, steady and unmoving, the same through all the changes of the world. In this passage the poem uses the four ancient elements to show how far the self lies beyond the reach of anything that can be touched or harmed.

To make the point clearer, Krishna offers an image that has become one of the best known in the whole poem. As a man gives up worn-out clothes and puts on others that are new, he says, so the embodied self gives up old bodies and takes on new ones. Death, seen in this light, becomes more like a change of clothing than an end.

The self, Krishna continues, is unmanifest, beyond the reach of thought and unchanging, and a person who understands it in this way has no reason to grieve. It cannot be seen as a body can be seen, nor measured as a thing can be measured, and yet it is more real than anything the eye can see. The teaching asks Arjuna to look past the surface, and to find his steadiness in what is deeper.

Suppose, Krishna says, that Arjuna does not accept this and believes that the self is constantly born and constantly dies, even then he should not grieve. Death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died, so it makes no sense to mourn what cannot be avoided. Krishna is patient enough to answer the doubter on his own ground, and not only the believer.

All beings, Krishna says, are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in the middle, and unmanifest again at their end, so what cause is there for lamenting? Everything we meet has come out of the unseen and will go back into it, like a morning mist that rises from a valley and fades. The thought is meant to be both humbling and consoling, because it places one grief in the larger rhythm of the world.

One person sees the self as a wonder, says Krishna, another speaks of it as a wonder and a third hears of it as a wonder, and yet even after hearing, no one truly knows it. The one who dwells in the body of every being is eternal and cannot be harmed, so Arjuna has no reason to mourn for any creature. With these words Krishna ends the first part of his answer, and he turns next to the question of duty.

Krishna now turns from the nature of the self to the question of what Arjuna should do, and he asks him to keep his own duty in view and not to tremble. For a warrior, he says, there is nothing better than a righteous battle, and fortunate are the fighters who find such a war come to them unsought, for it opens like a door to heaven. Behind these words stands the idea of dharma, the right order of things, which gives each person a role to fulfil.

If Arjuna now refuses to fight this lawful battle, Krishna warns, he will have thrown away both his duty and his good name, and he will have brought a burden upon himself. The argument is not meant as a threat but as a plain account of what his choice would mean for him and for those who depend on him. What Arjuna calls compassion may therefore be hiding a failure to act where action is needed.

People will tell the story of his disgrace for years to come, Krishna says, and for a man who has been honoured all his life, dishonour is worse than death. It is a hard saying, and it shows that Krishna knows how deeply a warrior's pride is bound up with his reputation. He is speaking to Arjuna in the language Arjuna knows best, before he begins to widen it.

The great chariot fighters, Krishna goes on, will think that Arjuna has withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and the men who once held him in high esteem will come to think little of him. His enemies will say many unspeakable things about his strength, and nothing could cause him more pain than that. In this way the teacher shows his pupil how his gentle conscience may look to others.

If Arjuna is killed in battle, Krishna says, he will reach heaven, and if he is victorious, he will enjoy the earth; either way, nothing is lost by standing firm. Therefore he must rise, resolved to fight, and put aside the doubt that has made him sit down in sorrow. The reasoning is plain, yet it is only the doorway to a much more subtle teaching that follows.

Now comes the key instruction, which Arjuna will hear again and again: treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat as the same, and then make ready for the fight. By acting with such an even mind, Krishna says, he will not incur sin, because the heart that is free from clinging cannot be stained by what the hands must do. This is the first glimpse of the teaching of balance that runs through the whole of the poem.

Krishna says that he has so far explained the wisdom of knowing the self, which the tradition calls sankhya, and that he will now explain the wisdom of yoga, the discipline of action. Armed with it, he promises, Arjuna will cast off the bondage that action brings. It is a hopeful message, because it suggests that a person need not escape from the world in order to be free within it.

On this path, Krishna assures him, no effort is wasted and no harm is done, so every step forward counts for something, however small. Even a little of this practice, he says, saves a person from great fear, and the fear that is meant is probably the fear of death itself. The verse has been a comfort for countless people who feel that they have only just begun.

The resolute mind, Krishna says, is single in its aim, while the minds of those who cannot decide are branched many times over and go off in endless directions. The image is almost visual, as of a straight arrow flying toward a target beside a handful of arrows scattered on the wind. Here the poem touches the problem Arjuna faces himself, for a divided mind is the very thing that has stopped him in his chariot.

There are some people of little understanding, Krishna says, who are fond of the flowery words of the scriptures and who say there is nothing else beyond them. Their hearts are full of desire, their goal is heaven, and the fine speeches they make promise pleasure and power in return for rituals, so their minds can never settle on a firm decision. It is a gentle warning against religion used as a way of getting things, rather than as a way of becoming free.

The ancient scriptures, Krishna says, deal with the three strands of nature, and Arjuna is urged to rise above them, free from the pairs of opposites, steady in the self, and unconcerned with gaining or keeping things. The mind that is tossed between pleasure and pain, praise and blame, is never at rest, so the first step toward peace is a kind of inner independence. These verses prepare for the most famous teaching of the whole poem, which comes immediately afterward.

You have a right to your actions, Krishna says, but never to their fruits, and this one sentence has been repeated by readers for many centuries as a summary of the whole Gita. It does not tell Arjuna to stop caring about what he does, for every action matters; it tells him to stop being ruled by the hope of reward and the fear of failure. A farmer sows his seed with great care, yet he cannot command the rain or the harvest that follows.

Do not let the results of your work be your motive, Krishna goes on, and do not fall into the habit of doing nothing either. Established in yoga, a person should perform actions after giving up attachment and treating success and failure as the same, for it is this evenness of mind that is called yoga. In a single breath the teaching rejects both frantic ambition and idle withdrawal, and it points the way between them.

Action performed for the sake of reward is far lower than action done with a steady mind, says Krishna, and those who work only for results are to be pitied. He advises Arjuna to take refuge in the wisdom of such evenness and then adds that yoga is skill in action. A craftsman who cares for the work itself, and not for the praise it brings, would understand him at once.

The wise who have united their minds with this steady wisdom give up the fruits of their actions, Krishna says, and so they are freed from the chain of birth and reach a state without sorrow. When Arjuna's mind has passed beyond the thicket of confusion, he will no longer be troubled by all that he has heard or will hear. Quietly, the poem moves from the problem of one battle toward the larger question of how a mind can be free.

At this point Arjuna asks the question that has been waiting in his mind, a question that the whole tradition has loved ever since. What is the sign of a person who is firmly established in wisdom, he wants to know, and how does such a person speak, sit and walk through the world? He wishes to see the ideal not only as an idea but as a living human being.

Krishna replies that a person is steady in wisdom when he gives up all the desires of the mind and finds contentment in the self alone. Such a person has no need to depend on outside things for happiness, because the source of joy has been discovered within. The portrait that follows is one of the great pictures of calm in world literature.

The one whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, and who has no craving for pleasure, is called a sage of steady mind, says Krishna, and passion, fear and anger have left him. He has no ties to anything that happens, and he neither rejoices at good fortune nor shrinks from bad. Even in this ancient description there is something recognisable and modern, for most people long to be less ruled by moods.

Krishna offers a picture that has become famous in many languages, saying that when the wise person draws the senses back from their objects, it is like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side. The senses are not destroyed, but they are brought under the mind's control, and so they cannot drag the person here and there. The image is calm and gentle, and it suggests that restraint can come from strength rather than from fear.

The objects of the senses turn away from the person who abstains from them, Krishna admits, but the taste for them remains, and only the sight of the highest truth makes even that taste disappear. He adds that the senses of even a striving, wise person can seize the mind by force and carry it away. It is an honest observation, and it explains why the Gita spends so long on the practical work of training the mind.

Krishna acknowledges how strong the senses are, for they are so restless that they can carry away the mind even of a wise person who is making a real effort. It is not enough to know the truth, he says, because the pull of the world is real, and so Arjuna must bring every sense under control. A controlled mind should then rest steadily on the highest, and in that rest it finds its strength.

In a famous passage, Krishna describes the slow chain by which a person is brought to ruin, beginning not with a wicked act but with a thought. When a man keeps dwelling on the objects of the senses, attachment to them is born, and from attachment springs desire, and from desire comes anger. Every step is small and quite natural, and that is precisely why the chain is so hard to notice.

From anger comes delusion, says Krishna, and from delusion comes the loss of memory, and when memory is lost the power of reason is destroyed. When reason is destroyed, the person is ruined, so a single burning desire can end by turning a whole life upside down. Anyone who has said something in a rage and regretted it for years will understand how true this picture is.

The person who moves among the objects of the senses with a disciplined mind, free from both attraction and aversion, wins a deep and settled serenity. In such serenity, Krishna says, all sorrows come to an end, and the mind of the person is soon firmly fixed. Peace, in this teaching, is not the absence of the world but a clear and steady way of meeting it.

The undisciplined person, Krishna says, has neither wisdom nor the power to meditate, and the one who cannot meditate has no peace, so how could such a person be happy? The question is asked gently, but it points to a hard truth about our restless age, in which people look for happiness everywhere except in a quiet mind. The poem insists that inner order has to come first, before any outer success can bring lasting satisfaction.

As the wind carries a ship away from its course on the water, Krishna says, so the wandering sense that the mind follows carries off a person's wisdom. A single unguarded desire is enough to change the direction of the whole voyage. The sailor in this image must therefore keep his hand on the rudder at all times.

A person whose senses are fully held back from their objects, Krishna says, stands firm in wisdom, because the mind is no longer scattered. What is night for all beings is a time of waking for the one who is self-controlled, and what is a time of waking for other beings is night for the sage who sees. The two groups live in the same world, yet they notice and value entirely different things.

Krishna gives another image, of an ocean that is filled from every side by rivers and yet remains unmoved, with its level undisturbed. In the same way, the person into whom all desires enter without disturbing his calm attains peace, whereas the person who chases after his desires never finds it. The sea is not empty of rivers, but it is not ruled by them, and that is the lesson.

The person who gives up all longing, and who moves through the world without a sense of ownership or of a separate, grasping self, wins true peace. He does not cling to the things he has, so he does not fear to lose them, and there is a lightness in him that others notice. Krishna is describing a freedom that does not depend on circumstances, wealth or the opinions of other people.

This, Krishna says, is the state of union with Brahman, the highest reality, and anyone who reaches it is never again deluded. Even if a person gains it only at the very end of life, he says, it brings freedom, so it is never too late to begin. With these words the second chapter, the longest of the first part, comes to its close.

Arjuna, still struggling, tells Krishna that if knowledge is considered higher than action, then he cannot see why Krishna is urging him toward this dreadful deed. Krishna's words, he says, seem to confuse his understanding, and so he asks for one clear answer by which he can reach what is best. The question is honest and direct, and it opens a chapter that becomes a manual of how to live in the world.

Krishna answers that two paths were taught in the beginning, the path of knowledge for those who prefer to reflect and the path of action for those who prefer to work. No one reaches freedom from action simply by refusing to act, he says, and no one attains perfection merely by giving up the world. The Gita does not reject renunciation, but it keeps asking what renunciation truly means for a person who must still live and work among others.

Not even for a moment, says Krishna, can anyone remain without acting, because the forces of nature compel every being to do something. The person who restrains the organs of action while the mind keeps brooding on sense objects is a self-deceiver, a pretender, but the one who guides the senses with the mind and works without attachment is far better. Duty then becomes a form of freedom, because it gives the restless mind something worthy to do, and so it is better than idleness in every way.

Work that is not done as an offering binds the person who does it, Krishna says, and so the right way is to work as a gift, free from attachment. He describes a great wheel in which giving sustains the world and the world sustains those who give, and he calls the person who takes everything and gives nothing a thief. Many readers have seen in this picture the idea that all living things depend on one another.

Kings such as Janaka, Krishna recalls, won perfection through action alone, and he tells Arjuna that he should act with a view to the welfare of the world. Whatever a great person does, others will do, and whatever standard he sets, the world follows. For an Arjuna who watches everyone around him, this is a heavy but important reminder that a leader's choices are never private.

Krishna now speaks of himself, telling Arjuna that there is no duty for him in the three worlds and nothing that he has not obtained, yet he continues to act. If he were to stop, he explains, people would follow his example everywhere, and the worlds would fall into ruin. It is a striking statement, for it suggests that the most perfect being is also the most active, but he acts without any need.

The ignorant act out of attachment to results, says Krishna, while the wise act for the welfare of the world, with no attachment of their own. The wise should not disturb the minds of those who do not yet understand, but should show by their own example how work is to be done well and with joy. This is the teacher's code of patience, and it applies as much to a parent or friend as to a sage.

Even a person of knowledge, Krishna says, acts in keeping with his own nature, because all beings follow their nature, and force cannot change it. The senses have their likes and dislikes, and these are the two great obstacles on the path, so one should not fall under their power. It is better to do your own duty imperfectly, he adds, than to do another person's duty well, because following another's path is full of danger.

Arjuna asks the question that all of us have asked, which is what drives a person to do wrong even when he does not want to, almost as if he were compelled. Krishna answers that it is desire, and anger born of desire, a devouring and sinful force which arises from the passionate strand of nature and which must be known as the enemy. It is a candid diagnosis, because it places the root of wrongdoing inside the self rather than outside.

As smoke covers fire, Krishna explains, and dust covers a mirror, and the womb covers the unborn child, so desire covers wisdom, and it burns like a fire that is never satisfied. Its seat is in the senses, the mind and the intellect, and so the way to defeat it is first to bring the senses under control and then to rely on mind and intellect. Beyond all of them stands the self, and by relying on it Arjuna can conquer the enemy that is hard to see.

Krishna tells Arjuna that he first taught this imperishable discipline of yoga to Vivasvan, the sun god, who passed it to Manu, the first lawgiver, and Manu gave it to the kings who followed. Through many generations, royal sages knew it, but in the long course of time it was lost to the world. Now Krishna has returned to teach it again, because Arjuna is both his friend and his devotee, and the teaching is a supreme secret.

Arjuna is astonished, because Vivasvan was born long before Krishna, so how, he asks, can he understand that Krishna taught the sun god in the beginning? Krishna answers calmly that both of them have passed through many births, and that while he remembers every one, Arjuna does not. This small exchange is the first hint in the Gita that the charioteer is more than he seems.

Though he is unborn and unchanging, and though he is lord of all beings, Krishna says, he comes into being through his own power, controlling his own nature. Whenever righteousness declines and wickedness grows strong, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good, to destroy evil and to establish dharma firmly. For millions of believers this is a promise that the world is never left without help, even in its darkest times.

The person who truly understands the divine nature of Krishna's birth and work does not take birth again, and many people, freed from attachment, fear and anger, have been purified by knowledge and have come to him. However people approach him, he welcomes them in the same way, for in the end all human paths lead toward him. The tradition has often quoted this verse to show the generous spirit of the teaching.

Those who long for quick success from their actions, Krishna says, worship the powers of nature, and success does come quickly to them in the human world. Yet actions do not stain him, for he has no longing for their results, and anyone who knows him in this way is not bound by actions either. The wise of ancient times acted with this very understanding, and Krishna urges Arjuna to follow their example.

What action is, and what inaction is, confuses even the wise, Krishna says, and he promises to explain it. He then declares that the one who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among people. It is a paradox that has inspired a great deal of thought, since it suggests that a busy person can be inwardly still and an idle person inwardly restless.

The wise person, Krishna says, has no desire in any of his undertakings, because his actions have been burned in the fire of knowledge, and he gives up attachment to their results. He is content with whatever comes by chance, free of envy, beyond the pairs of opposites, and the same in success and in failure, so even when he acts, he is not bound. The portrait is full of calm dignity, and it makes a quiet argument that work and peace can live together.

Many kinds of sacrifice are spread out in the sacred tradition, says Krishna, for some people offer wealth, some practise severe discipline, some study sacred texts, and others control their breath or the senses. All of them, he says, are people who know what sacrifice is and are cleansed of sin by it, but he declares that the sacrifice of knowledge is greater than any sacrifice of objects. For all action, he adds, finds its fulfilment in knowledge, which is the quiet goal toward which every kind of sacrifice is pointing.

Krishna advises Arjuna to learn this knowledge by bowing humbly to those who have seen the truth, by asking them questions and by serving them, and they will teach him. When he has understood, he will not fall into confusion again, and he will see all beings in himself and in Krishna. Even if he were the worst of sinners, he adds, he would cross over all wrongdoing by the boat of knowledge.

As a blazing fire reduces wood to ashes, Krishna says, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes, and nothing in this world purifies like knowledge. Faith, self-control and devotion bring it, he says, but the doubter, who has neither faith nor understanding, is lost and finds no happiness here or elsewhere. Therefore Arjuna must cut through the doubt in his heart with the sword of knowledge, take refuge in yoga, and rise to his feet.

Arjuna, who has been listening closely, puts a hard question to Krishna that he has not been able to settle for himself. You praise the giving up of action, he says, and then you praise the yoga of action, so tell me clearly which of the two is better. Krishna answers that both lead to the highest, but that of the two, the yoga of action is better than the giving up of action.

A true renouncer, Krishna says, is not someone who has run away from the world but someone who neither hates nor desires, and so is free from the pairs of opposites and is easily released from bondage. Only children, not the wise, speak of knowledge and action as being different, for whoever is truly established in one reaches the fruit of both. In this way the poem tries to heal what looks like a quarrel between two great paths.

The one who knows the truth, Krishna says, thinks to himself that he does nothing at all, even while he is seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing. He understands that these are merely the senses moving among their own objects, and he is not carried away by a sense of being the great doer of everything he does. It is a subtle thought, for it asks the reader to take part in the world while keeping a certain light distance from it.

Whoever acts, offering all actions to the highest and giving up attachment, Krishna says, is not touched by wrong, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by the water on which it floats. The leaf is always in the pond, but the water never clings to it, and that is the whole image. It has become one of the most loved pictures of the Gita because it shows that a person can live fully in the world and still stay pure.

The self, Krishna says, rests contentedly in the body like a king in a city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing others to act, since it is nature that does the work. Ignorance covers wisdom and so beings are bewildered, but for those in whom knowledge has destroyed ignorance, it shines like the sun and reveals what is highest. The nine gates are traditionally understood as the openings of the body, and the image makes the body a home rather than a prison.

The wise, says Krishna, look with an equal eye on a learned and humble scholar, a cow, an elephant and a dog, and also on those whom society despises. Even in this world, he says, those whose minds are fixed in equality have conquered rebirth, because the highest reality is flawless and the same in all. This verse is often quoted in India as a call to respect every living being.

The person who is not delighted when something pleasant comes and not disturbed when something unpleasant comes, Krishna says, stays steady, clear in mind and unconfused. Pleasures that are born of contact with the senses are wombs of pain, because they have a beginning and an end, so the wise do not delight in them. The one who is able to withstand the rush of desire and anger before leaving the body is a true yogi and is truly happy.

The person who finds happiness within, and rest within, and light within, Krishna says, becomes a yogi and reaches peace in the highest. Sages whose faults have been destroyed and whose doubts have been cut, who rejoice in the welfare of all beings, find that freedom is close at hand. Those who know Krishna as the friend of all beings and the lord of all the worlds, he promises, attain peace.

Krishna returns to the question of renunciation, saying that the true renouncer is not the person who lights no sacred fire and does no work, but the one who does his duty without depending on its results. For the seeker who wishes to climb to yoga, action is the means, he says, while for the one who has already climbed, calm and stillness are the means. In this way the poem teaches that the path itself changes as a person grows.

Let a person lift himself by his own self, says Krishna, and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is also the enemy of the self. For the one who has conquered the self, it is a friend; for the one who has not, it behaves like an enemy. The yogi who is satisfied by knowledge sees a lump of clay, a stone and gold as the same, and treats friends, enemies, the good and the wicked with the same evenness of mind.

Krishna now speaks about the practice of meditation, beginning with the setting, and he says that the yogi should live alone in a quiet place, with his mind and body controlled and free from longing and from owning things. He should prepare a clean spot and set up for himself a firm seat that is neither too high nor too low, covered with grass, a skin and cloth. Seated there, with his mind gathered on one point and his senses calm, he should practise yoga for the purification of the self.

The yogi should hold his body, head and neck steady and upright, Krishna says, and he should fix his gaze without looking about in every direction. With a peaceful heart, free from fear, he should sit with his mind controlled and fixed on Krishna, who is his highest goal. The person who practises in this way, always joining his mind with the highest, comes to a peace that rests in Krishna himself.

Yoga is not for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who does not eat at all, Krishna says, nor for the one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. For the person who is moderate in eating, in recreation, in action, and in sleeping and waking, yoga destroys all sorrow. It is a refreshingly practical teaching, and it suggests that spiritual discipline is a matter of balance and not of extremes.

When the mind is fully controlled and rests in the self alone, free from every craving, the yogi is said to be steady, and Krishna explains it with one of the best images in the poem. As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so the controlled mind of a yogi who practises union with the self stays unmoved. The picture is so quiet and concrete that readers have remembered it for centuries.

Where the mind, quieted by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and where the yogi sees the self by the self and finds contentment, there he knows an infinite joy that the senses cannot reach. Once established in that joy, he never moves away from the truth, and having gained it, he thinks there is no greater gain, and he is not shaken even by the heaviest sorrow. This yoga, Krishna says, is to be practised with firm determination and with a mind that does not lose heart.

Krishna tells Arjuna to abandon without exception all the desires born of imagination and to restrain the senses on every side by the mind alone. Little by little, with an intellect held steady, the yogi should gain tranquillity, with his mind fixed on the self and thinking of nothing else. Wherever the restless and unsteady mind wanders, he should draw it back and bring it again under the control of the self, and to the yogi whose mind is thus peaceful, the highest bliss comes.

The one who has become steadfast in yoga sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, Krishna says, and he sees the same everywhere. Whoever sees Krishna in everything and sees everything in Krishna is never lost to him, nor is Krishna ever lost to that person. The highest yogi, Krishna adds, is the one who judges everything by the standard of his own self, feeling the pleasure and the pain of others as if they were his own.

Arjuna says frankly that he cannot see how this steady yoga could last, because the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, and holding it back is as hard as holding back the wind. Krishna agrees without any hesitation that the mind is hard to restrain and always moving, and then he adds that it can be held by practice and by detachment. Yoga is difficult for the unrestrained self, he says, but it can be reached by anyone who strives with the proper means.

Arjuna now asks what happens to a person who has faith but cannot keep control of the mind, whose thoughts wander away from yoga so that he fails to reach perfection. Does such a person perish like a torn cloud, he wonders, lost on both paths and with nothing to stand on? Krishna replies tenderly that there is no destruction for him in this world or the next, because no one who does good ever comes to a bad end.

The failed yogi, Krishna says, reaches the worlds of the good, lives there for many years and is then reborn in a pure and prosperous family, or even in the family of wise yogis. There he regains the knowledge of his former life and strives again, and by effort through many births he is purified and finally reaches the highest goal. The yogi is greater than those who practise severe discipline, greater than the learned and greater than those who perform rituals, and therefore, Krishna says, be a yogi, Arjuna.

Krishna promises to explain to Arjuna the knowledge that is joined to direct experience, so that, when he has understood it, nothing more will remain to be known. Among thousands of people, he says, perhaps one strives for perfection, and of those who strive and succeed, hardly one knows him in his true nature. The seventh chapter begins with a gentle warning that this is rare and precious knowledge.

Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego are the eight parts of his nature, Krishna says, but this is only his lower nature, for there is another and higher one, the living spirit that supports the world. All beings come from these two, and he is both the beginning and the end of the whole world. There is nothing higher than he, and everything hangs on him like rows of pearls on a single thread.

Krishna names how he can be found in the world, and he does it in a series of vivid pictures. He is the taste in water, the light of the moon and the sun, the sacred sound Om in the Vedas, the sound in space, and the strength of those who are strong, free of passion. He is also the pure fragrance in the earth, the brightness in fire, the life in all beings, and the eternal seed of everything that grows.

The three strands of nature come from Krishna, he says, yet he is not in them but beyond them, and the whole world, deluded by these three, does not know him. This divine power of illusion, which is made of the three strands, is very hard to cross; but those who take refuge in Krishna alone cross it. The evil and the deluded do not turn to him, because their knowledge has been carried away by illusion.

Four kinds of good people worship Krishna, he says, the person in distress, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth and the wise person, who is the best of them because he is always steady in his devotion. All are noble, but the wise one is dearest, for Krishna is exceedingly dear to him and he to Krishna. After many births, the wise person comes to him, knowing that all that exists is the divine, and such a great soul is very rare.

Those whose knowledge has been carried away by desires turn to other powers, Krishna says, and he himself makes their faith steady, so they receive what they long for, although those rewards are limited. Veiled by his own divine power, he is not revealed to everyone, and the deluded world does not know him who is unborn and imperishable. Yet the people of good deeds whose sin has ended, freed from the confusion of opposites, worship him with a firm resolve.

At the start of the eighth chapter, Arjuna asks seven questions at once, about Brahman, the self, action, the material and divine realms, the lord of sacrifice and how Krishna is known at the hour of death. Krishna answers that Brahman is the imperishable highest reality, that the self is its nature in each being, and that he himself is the lord of sacrifice in the body. It is a brief reply, but the rest of the chapter unfolds it at much greater length and with great care.

Whoever leaves the body at the end of life, remembering Krishna alone, Krishna says, reaches him without doubt, and whatever state a person remembers at the end, that state he reaches. For that reason he tells Arjuna to remember him at all times and to fight, and with a mind and intellect fixed on him, he will certainly come to him. A life of steady remembrance, rather than a last-minute prayer, is the real teaching here.

Krishna says that all the worlds, up to the realm of the creator Brahma, are subject to return, but whoever reaches him is not born again. A day of Brahma lasts a thousand ages and so does his night, and at the dawn of each day all things come forth from the unmanifest and at nightfall they dissolve into it again. Beyond that unmanifest, he says, there is another eternal existence which does not perish when all beings perish, and from it there is no return.

Krishna describes two paths by which yogis depart this world, one of fire, light and day, the other of smoke and night. One leads to no return and the other to return, and the yogi who knows these paths is not confused, so Arjuna must always be steady in yoga. Such a yogi goes beyond the rewards of study, sacrifice, austerity and charity, and reaches the supreme original abode.

Krishna now promises to share with Arjuna, who does not find fault with him, the most secret knowledge, joined with direct experience, and when it is known, he says, Arjuna will be freed from all evil. This royal knowledge is a royal secret, supremely pure, easy to practise and imperishable, and it can be directly seen. Those without faith in it, however, do not reach Krishna and return to the cycle of birth and death.

This whole world, Krishna says, is pervaded by him in his unseen form, and all beings rest in him, but he does not rest in them. Behold my divine power, he says, for although I support all beings, I am not in them, and as the mighty wind that moves everywhere rests always in space, so all beings rest in me. The paradox is deliberate, because it points to a being who is at once the ground of everything and untouched by anything.

At the end of an age, all beings enter Krishna's nature, he explains, and at the beginning of the next he sends them forth again, ruling over his own nature. This whole multitude is helpless under nature's power, but these acts do not bind him, because he sits as one who is indifferent and unattached. Under his watchful eye, nature produces everything that moves and everything that does not, and so the world turns.

Fools disregard Krishna when he has taken a human form, for they do not know his higher nature as the great Lord of all beings. Their hopes, their actions and their knowledge are all in vain, and they fall into a deluded nature. By contrast, the great souls, who have a divine nature, know him as the imperishable source of all and worship him with minds that look nowhere else.

Krishna says he is the ritual, the sacrifice, the offering made for the ancestors, the healing herb, the sacred word, the clarified butter, the fire and the offering itself. He is the father and the mother of this world, its supporter and its grandfather, the sacred syllable Om, the goal, the friend, the witness and the refuge. He gives heat, he holds back the rain and sends it forth, and he is both immortality and death.

Those who follow the rituals of the scriptures in hope of heaven enjoy its pleasures for a time, Krishna says, but when their merit is used up they return to the world of mortals. For those who worship him alone, thinking of nothing else and constantly united with him, he carries what they lack and preserves what they have. The two promises together describe a trust that is both practical and deeply personal.

In one of the most tender verses of the Gita, Krishna says that if someone offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts that offering of love from a person of pure heart. The gift itself could not be simpler, and anybody can find it, however poor, and so no one is shut out. What counts is not the value of the thing offered but the devotion with which it is given.

Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, and whatever discipline you practise, Krishna says to Arjuna, do it as an offering to me. In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action, which bear good and bad results, and with your mind joined to the yoga of renunciation, you will come to me. This turns every ordinary act, even a meal, into a possible form of worship.

I am equal to all beings, Krishna says, and none is hateful or dear to me, but those who worship me with devotion are in me and I am in them. Even if a person of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he must be considered righteous, because he has made the right resolve, and soon he becomes a person of virtue and finds lasting peace. Krishna ends the verse with a promise that is meant to reach every doubting heart, that his devotee is never lost.

Even those whom society regards as lowly, Krishna says, whether women, merchants or labourers, can reach the highest goal if they take refuge in him, and how much more, then, can the pious and the royal sages. Since Arjuna has been born into this fleeting and joyless world, he should worship Krishna, fix his mind on him, be devoted to him and bow to him. Thus joined to him, with Krishna as his supreme goal, he will come to him.

Krishna says that he will speak again to Arjuna, who is so dear to him, in order that he may do him good, and he calls the teaching his supreme word. Neither the hosts of the gods nor the great sages know his origin, for he is the source of gods and sages alike. The person who knows him as unborn, without beginning and the great Lord of the worlds, he says, is free of delusion among mortals and free of all sins.

Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from confusion, patience, truth, self-control and calm, Krishna says, together with pleasure and pain, birth and death, fear and fearlessness, all come from him alone. So do non-violence, evenness of mind, contentment, charity and fame, as well as their opposites, which means that the whole range of human experience has the same single source. Even the seven great sages and the Manus were born from his mind, and from them came all the creatures of the world.

Those who know in truth his glory and his power, Krishna says, become united with him by a firm and unshaken yoga, and the wise who understand that he is the source of all worship him with love. With their minds fixed on him and their lives given to him, they enlighten one another and speak of him always, and they are content and rejoice. To these devoted ones Krishna gives the understanding by which they come to him, and out of pure compassion he destroys the darkness of ignorance in their hearts with the shining lamp of knowledge.

Arjuna now speaks, moved to the depths, and calls Krishna the supreme Brahman, the supreme home and the supreme purifier, the eternal divine person, the first of the gods, unborn and all-pervading. All the sages say so, he adds, including Narada, Asita and Vyasa, and now Krishna himself says it to him. He asks Krishna to describe, without holding anything back, the divine glories by which he fills these worlds, because he is never tired of hearing his words, which are like nectar.

Krishna agrees to tell Arjuna of his chief divine glories, since there is no end to the details of them. He begins at the closest point of all, saying that he is the self that dwells in the hearts of all beings, and that he is the beginning, the middle and also the end of every creature. It is a typical move in this chapter, for the greatest powers of the universe are traced back to the quiet centre in each person.

Among lights Krishna is the radiant sun, and among the stars he is the moon, and then he moves through the world, naming in every class of things the one that is greatest. Among the senses he is the mind, among living beings he is consciousness, among mountains he is the great Meru, and among bodies of water he is the ocean. Among words he is the single syllable Om, and among the things that cannot move, he is the Himalayas.

Among trees he is the sacred banyan, Krishna goes on, among beasts the lion, among rivers the Ganges and among those who purify the wind. Among men he is the king, among the heavenly sages Narada, and among the wise Kapila, who is remembered as a great teacher. The list is not a ranking of the world, but a way of showing how the divine can be seen shining out of many different kinds of things.

Of all creations Krishna is the beginning, the middle and the end, he says, and among the sciences he is the knowledge of the self. Among the seasons he is spring, among splendid things he is their splendour, and he is also victory, effort and the goodness of the good. He is the courage of the brave, and he is time itself, which never runs out, and in this way he points to every part of life as a doorway to the divine.

Among the Pandavas, Krishna says, he is Arjuna himself, and among the sages he is Vyasa, who is the author of the Mahabharata according to tradition. Among secrets he is silence, and among the wise he is wisdom, and in saying so he honours quiet and understanding above any show of power. Arjuna, listening on the battlefield, finds himself in the list, and he cannot help but feel both honoured and humbled.

Whatever is the seed of all beings, Krishna declares, he is that, and nothing moving or unmoving can exist without him. There is no end to his divine glories, he says, and what he has named is only a brief sample, for anything that is glorious, prosperous or powerful has come from a small fragment of his splendour. But what use to Arjuna is such detailed knowledge, he asks, when with a single fragment of himself he supports this entire universe?

Arjuna says that the words about the highest secret, which Krishna spoke out of kindness, have removed his confusion, for he has heard in detail of the arising and the passing away of all beings. Now he wants to see with his own eyes the divine form of which Krishna has spoken, and he asks, if Krishna thinks it possible, to be shown the imperishable self. This is the greatest request in the poem, and it is made with respect and a little fear.

Krishna tells him to look upon forms by the hundreds and the thousands, of many kinds and colours and shapes, and to see the gods and many wonders that no one has seen before. The whole universe, moving and unmoving, will be seen standing in one place in his body, he says, but Arjuna cannot see it with these eyes of his own. So Krishna gives him a divine eye, and in this way a chariot on a battlefield becomes a doorway to infinity.

Sanjaya, who is reporting everything to the blind king, says that Krishna then showed his supreme divine form, with countless mouths and eyes, many wonderful sights, and many divine ornaments and raised weapons. If the radiance of a thousand suns were to burst forth at once in the sky, he says, it might be like the splendour of that great being. In it Arjuna saw the entire universe, divided in a thousand ways, gathered together in one place.

Arjuna, amazed and with his hair standing on end, bows with joined hands and says that he sees all the gods in Krishna's body, with every kind of being, the creator Brahma seated on his lotus, and the sages. He sees arms, bellies, mouths and eyes without number, and no beginning, middle or end to the form. It is a blazing mass of light, hard to look at, and he knows that Krishna is the imperishable, the supreme to be known, the guardian of eternal dharma.

Arjuna sees Krishna without beginning, middle or end, with endless power and arms without number, with the sun and the moon as his eyes and a burning fire for his mouth, heating the whole universe with his light. The space between heaven and earth and all the directions are filled by him alone, and seeing this wonderful and terrible form, the three worlds tremble. Hosts of gods enter into him, and some fold their hands in fear and praise him, and the sages and the perfect cry out for peace.

Seeing Krishna touching the sky, blazing in many colours, with wide open mouths and large fiery eyes, Arjuna's inner self trembles, and he finds neither courage nor peace. The fearful mouths with their great teeth look like the fire at the end of time, and he loses all sense of direction and finds no comfort. In this passage a hero who has faced many armies without a tremor is reduced to a helpless prayer for mercy.

All the sons of Dhritarashtra, with the crowds of kings, Bhishma, Drona and Karna, and the chief warriors of Arjuna's side as well, are seen rushing into the blazing mouths. As many rivers run toward the ocean, and as moths rush into a burning flame to be consumed, so these heroes enter the mouths of the great form, licking and burning all the worlds with its rays. Arjuna cries, tell me who you are in this terrible form, for I do not understand what you are about to do.

I am Time, the great destroyer of the worlds, Krishna replies, and I have come here to bring the worlds to their end. Even without you, none of the warriors in the opposing armies will live, so rise up and win glory, for they have already been slain by me, and you must only be my instrument. Do not be afraid, he adds, for Bhishma, Drona and Karna are already defeated by me, and you will conquer your foes.

Trembling, with joined hands, Arjuna bows again and speaks in a choked voice, praising Krishna as the original god, the refuge of the universe, the imperishable, the knower and the thing to be known.
