He begs forgiveness for every time that he called Krishna by his name, as a friend, in jest, at play or at rest, not knowing his greatness, and asks to be forgiven as a father forgives a son. Delighted, yet shaken by fear, he asks to see Krishna's former form again, with crown, mace and discus, or his gentle human form.

Krishna says that by his own power and favour he has shown Arjuna this supreme, shining, infinite and primeval form, which no one other than Arjuna has ever seen. It cannot be seen by study of the Vedas, nor by sacrifices, gifts, rituals or fierce discipline, he says, and he tells Arjuna not to be afraid or confused by the terrible sight. Then Krishna, having spoken, showed again his own form, and the great soul, becoming gentle once more, comforted the frightened Arjuna.

Seeing again the gentle human form of Krishna, Arjuna says that his mind is now collected and he has returned to his own nature, and the relief in his voice is clear. Krishna replies that the form Arjuna has seen is very hard to see, and that even the gods are always longing to see it. After the vast and terrible vision, it is the friend's ordinary face that restores Arjuna's peace.

Neither by the Vedas, nor by hard discipline, nor by gifts or by sacrifices, Krishna says, can he be seen in the form that Arjuna has seen, but only by undivided devotion can he be known and truly entered. The person who works for Krishna, who has him as the highest goal, who is devoted to him and free from attachment and from hatred toward any being, will come to him. With these words the eleventh chapter ends, with a promise that is open to everyone.

Arjuna now asks a practical question, which is whether those who worship Krishna steadily with devotion, or those who worship the imperishable and unseen, are the better yogis. Krishna answers that he considers best those who fix their minds on him and worship him with supreme faith. The question is an old one, about whether God is better approached through a personal form or through the formless, and Krishna answers with gentleness and not with argument.

Those who worship the imperishable, unseen and unthinkable, with senses controlled and joy in the welfare of all, also reach Krishna, he says, but the path of the unmanifest is harder for those who are in a body. For those who place all their actions in him and worship him with single-minded yoga, he soon becomes the one who lifts them from the ocean of birth and death. The image of the rescuer reaching down to a swimmer is one of the warmest in the poem.

Krishna gives a ladder of steps, so that every person can start from where he or she is. If you can fix your mind on me, do so, he says; if you cannot, try to reach me by constant practice, and if that is too hard, do your work for my sake. If even that is impossible, take refuge in me and give up the fruits of all actions, for he adds that peace follows at once from such giving up.

The devotee who is dear to Krishna, he says, hates no being, is friendly and compassionate, and has no sense of ownership or of ego, and he is the same in pain and pleasure and forgiving toward others. He is always content, self-controlled and firm in his resolve, and he does not disturb the world, nor is he disturbed by it. This portrait goes on to praise one who is equal in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat, and in praise and blame, silent, content and steady.

The thirteenth chapter begins with Krishna telling Arjuna that this body is called the field, and that the one who knows it is called the knower of the field by those who understand these things. He adds that he himself is the knower of the field in all fields, and that the knowledge of the field and of the knower is, in his view, true knowledge. In this way the Gita turns from the world outside to the mystery of who is looking at it.

Krishna lists what makes up the field, namely the great elements, the ego, the intellect and the unmanifest source, the ten senses and the mind, and the five objects of the senses. It also includes desire, hatred, pleasure and pain, the body as a whole, intelligence and firmness, and he says that this is the field, together with all its changes. A modern reader will recognise in this list both the body and much of what we call personality and emotion.

Krishna explains that real knowledge is made of humility, freedom from pretence, harmlessness, patience, honesty, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness and self-control. It also means turning away from the pleasure of the senses, seeing the pain of birth, death, old age and sickness, and keeping an equal mind amid wanted and unwanted things. Above all, it is unswerving devotion to Krishna, and everything that is opposed to it, he says, is ignorance.

What must be known, Krishna says, is the highest reality, which has no beginning and is said to be neither being nor non-being, and which has hands, feet, eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, because it dwells in everything. It shines through all the senses without having senses, supports all beings without being attached, and is outside and inside all things, too subtle to be seen, and both far away and near. It is the light of all lights, beyond darkness, and it sits in the hearts of everyone.

Nature and the spirit are both without beginning, Krishna says, and all changes and qualities are born of nature, which is the cause of every effect. The spirit, seated in nature, is what experiences pleasure and pain, and the supreme person in the body is the witness, the one who permits, the supporter, the enjoyer and the great Lord. It is a profound distinction between what acts and what watches, and it is the foundation of much later Indian philosophy.

The one who knows this spirit and nature with its strands, Krishna says, is not born again, however he may live, and the paths to such knowledge are many. Some people see the self in themselves by meditation, others by knowledge, others by action, and others, who do not know, hear about it from teachers and worship with faith, and they too cross beyond death. Whoever sees the supreme Lord dwelling equally in all beings does not harm the self by the self, and so goes to the highest goal.

The one who sees that all actions are done by nature alone, and that the self is not the doer, truly sees, says Krishna. When he sees the variety of beings as rooted in one and spreading from it, he reaches Brahman. As space is never stained, because it is so subtle, so the self seated in every body is never stained; and as one sun lights up the whole world, the lord of the field lights up the whole field.

Krishna begins the fourteenth chapter by promising to speak again of the supreme knowledge, the best of all knowledge, by which all the sages have gone from this world to the highest perfection. Those who have taken refuge in this knowledge, he says, are not born again at the beginning of creation, nor are they disturbed at the time of dissolution. The great Brahman is his womb, he says, and in it he places the seed, and from this all beings are born.

Sattva, rajas and tamas, Krishna explains, are the three strands of nature, and they bind the imperishable self to the body. Sattva is pure, bright and healthy, and it binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge, while rajas is passion, born of craving, and it binds by attachment to action. Tamas, born of ignorance, deludes all beings and binds them by heedlessness, laziness and sleep, and in every person all three are always at work.

Each strand, Krishna says, rises by overcoming the other two, and so a person's nature changes from time to time as one or another takes the lead. When the light of knowledge shines through every gate of the body, he says, sattva is strong, while greed, restless activity and craving point to rajas, and darkness and confusion mean tamas has risen. The results differ too, for sattva leads upward, rajas leaves a person in the middle, and tamas drags him down.

When a person sees that there is no actor other than the strands, and knows that which is beyond them, Krishna says, he enters into Krishna's own being. He is not bothered when light, activity or delusion arise, nor does he long for them when they cease, and he is the same in pain and pleasure, and in praise and blame. Whoever serves Krishna with unfailing devotion crosses beyond the three strands and is fit to become Brahman.

Krishna speaks of the world as an everlasting tree, with its roots above and its branches below, and its leaves are the sacred hymns. Its branches spread up and down, fed by the three strands, and its twigs are the objects of the senses, while its roots reach down into the world of human action. Its form cannot be seen clearly here, but one must cut this deeply rooted tree with the strong axe of detachment, and then seek the place from which those who reach it never return.

An eternal part of Krishna himself, he says, becomes the living self in the world of living beings, drawing to itself the mind and the five senses that rest in nature. When the ruler of the body leaves it, or enters another, it takes these along with it, as the wind carries scents away from their place of origin. The deluded do not see it, whether it departs or stays, whether it enjoys or is joined to the strands, but those who have the eye of knowledge do see.

The light of the sun that brightens the whole world, and the light in the moon and in the fire, are all his, says Krishna, and he enters the earth and supports beings with his strength. He becomes the fire of digestion in the bodies of living beings, he sits in the hearts of all, and from him come memory, knowledge and also their loss. Because he is beyond the perishable and higher than even the imperishable, he is called the highest person, and one who knows him worships him with all his heart.

Krishna now lists the qualities of those born with a divine nature, and the list is long and gentle: fearlessness, purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge and yoga, charity, self-control, study and straightforwardness. It continues with non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquillity and compassion for all beings, followed by gentleness, modesty, vigour, forgiveness and fortitude. Last of all come purity and freedom from malice and from pride, which are the marks of a person who is born to a divine state.

The qualities of the ungodly nature, Krishna says, are hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance, and the divine qualities lead to freedom, while the ungodly lead to bondage. Then he comforts Arjuna with a tender sentence, saying that he should not grieve, for he was born with the divine qualities. The chapter seems to be a mirror in which the reader is invited to look at his or her own character with honesty and without despair.

There are people, says Krishna, who do not know what should be done and what should be avoided, and in whom there is neither purity nor right conduct nor truth. Filled with endless desires, they cling to bad ideas and think that gratifying their wishes is the highest goal of life. They boast that they have gained this today and will gain that tomorrow, and that no one is their equal, and deluded in this way, they are bound by hundreds of ties of hope.

There are three gates to the self-destruction of the soul, says Krishna, and they are desire, anger and greed, so a wise person must give them up. The one who is freed from these three dark gates does what is good for himself and so moves toward the highest goal. Whoever ignores the teaching and follows his own whims finds neither happiness nor success nor peace, so let the scripture be your guide, he says, in deciding what ought to be done.

Arjuna asks a fair question about those who offer worship with faith but do not follow the rules of the scriptures, and wonders whether their faith belongs to goodness, passion or darkness. Krishna answers that faith is of three kinds, according to a person's nature, and he adds that a person is made of his faith, so whatever a man's faith is, that he is. The idea is bold, for it suggests that what we believe in shapes the person we become.

The people of goodness worship the gods, Krishna says, the people of passion worship powers of wealth and force, and the people of darkness worship spirits of the dead. There are also those who practise terrible austerities not recommended by any scripture, driven by hypocrisy, ego, desire and force, and these people torment the elements of the body and also Krishna himself, who lives within. Krishna calls them mistaken in their resolve, for true strength does not need to hurt the body.

The food that each person likes is also of three kinds, Krishna says, and so are sacrifice, discipline and giving. The food of goodness increases life, purity, strength, health, happiness and joy, being juicy, rich and agreeable, while the food of passion is bitter, sour, salty, burning and harsh, causing pain, grief and disease. The food of darkness is stale, tasteless, rotten and left over, and the point seems to be that our choices at the table are another place where our nature shows.

Sacrifice offered according to the rules, by those who do not want a reward and who feel that it is simply a duty to do it, is of the nature of goodness, Krishna says. The sacrifice offered for the sake of reward, or for show, is of the nature of passion, while the one done against the rules, without sharing food, sacred words, gifts or faith, is of the nature of darkness. In plain words, the same act can be high or low depending on its reason.

Krishna describes the discipline of the body as honouring gods, teachers and the wise, along with purity, straightforwardness and non-violence. The discipline of speech is to speak words that cause no distress and are truthful, pleasant and helpful, and the discipline of the mind is calm, gentleness, silence, self-control and purity of heart. Done with faith and without desire for reward, he says, such discipline is of the nature of goodness, and these verses have often been quoted as a simple guide to daily life.

A gift that is given because it is a duty, with no thought of return, at the right place and time, to a person who deserves it, is a gift of goodness, Krishna says. A gift given in hope of something in return, or grudgingly, is of passion, and one given in the wrong place and time, to the wrong person, with contempt, is of darkness. The sacred words Om Tat Sat, he concludes, name the highest reality, and any sacrifice, gift or discipline done without faith is called asat, worthless in this world and in the next.

Arjuna now asks Krishna to explain the truth of renunciation and of relinquishment, and how the two differ. Krishna replies that sages call the giving up of actions that spring from desire renunciation, while the wise call the giving up of the fruits of every action relinquishment. Some thinkers, he adds, say that all action should be given up as an evil, but others say that sacrifice, giving and discipline should never be abandoned.

Krishna gives his own judgement, saying that acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline should not be given up but should be performed, because they purify even the wise. They must be done, however, with attachment and the desire for their fruits set aside, for that is his firm and highest opinion. In this way the Gita rescues ordinary duties from the suspicion that they are obstacles to the spiritual life.

To give up one's obligatory duty is not proper, Krishna says, for giving it up out of confusion is a dark kind of renunciation, and giving it up because it is painful is a restless kind that brings no reward. The best kind of relinquishment is to perform a duty simply because it ought to be done, giving up attachment to it and to its fruits. No embodied being can give up all action, he says, but the one who gives up the fruit of action is truly called a relinquisher.

There are five causes that bring about any action, Krishna says, which are the body, the doer, the various senses, the many kinds of effort and, as the fifth, the unseen power of destiny. Whatever a person does with body, speech or mind, rightly or wrongly, these five are the causes, and so the one who thinks that his self alone is the doer does not see rightly. A person who is free from the sense of being the doer, and whose mind is not tainted, is not bound by what he does.

Knowledge, Krishna says, is of three kinds, and the best is that by which a person sees one imperishable reality in all beings, undivided in the divided. The kind that sees many separate natures in all beings as distinct belongs to passion, and the kind that clings to one small thing as if it were the whole, without reason, belongs to darkness. The difference between them is one of breadth, for the more a person sees, the less he is shut up in his own small corner.

Action is of three kinds as well, he says, and so is the doer, and Krishna describes each with a short portrait. The best action is done as a duty, without attachment and without love or hatred, and the best doer is free from attachment and ego, firm, eager and unmoved by success or failure. The restless doer is driven by desire and greed, and the dark one is unsteady, stubborn, lazy and given to putting things off, which many people will recognise in themselves on some days.

The best intellect, Krishna says, knows what ought to be done and what ought not, what is to be feared and what is not, and what binds a person and what sets him free. The restless intellect confuses right with wrong, and the dark intellect, wrapped in ignorance, takes wrong for right and sees everything upside down. Steadfastness, which holds the mind, breath and senses in yoga, is of three kinds as well, and it is best when it is firm, unwavering and pure.

Krishna says that happiness is of three kinds, and he describes the best in a way that has stayed in readers' minds. It is like poison at first but like nectar in the end, born from the serenity of a mind turned to the self, while happiness from the senses is sweet at first and bitter at the end. The lowest kind, born of sleep, laziness and carelessness, deceives from start to finish, and no being on earth or among the gods is free from the strands.

In the language of its time, the Gita speaks of four groups of people, each with duties that fit its own nature, from calm learning and courageous leadership to farming, trade and service. The point Krishna makes is that each person is made for some kind of work, and that devotion to that work, and not a comparison with the work of others, leads to perfection. Readers today often discuss how far these lines describe a social order and how far they describe a person's own gifts.

Devoted to his own duty, each person attains perfection, says Krishna, and the way is by honouring through his own work the one from whom all beings arise and by whom the whole world is pervaded. It is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than another's duty well, he says, and a person who does the work set by his nature does not incur sin. Every undertaking, in fact, is covered by some fault, as a fire is by smoke, so work should not be abandoned merely because it is flawed.

The person whose intellect is free from attachment everywhere, who has mastered himself and who has no desire, reaches by renunciation the highest freedom from action, Krishna says. He then shows how such a person reaches Brahman, through a purified mind, firm resolve, a simple life in solitude, light eating and control of speech, body and mind. Constant meditation, freedom from ego, pride, desire, anger and possessions, and a peaceful heart make that person ready to become one with Brahman.

Having become one with Brahman, the person is serene, Krishna says, neither grieving nor craving, equal toward all beings, and he attains supreme devotion to Krishna. By devotion he knows Krishna in truth, what he is and who he is, and having known him in truth, he enters into him without delay. It is a description of a path that begins with duty and discipline and ends in love.

Even though he does all kinds of actions, Krishna says, the person who takes refuge in him reaches by his grace the eternal and imperishable home. So Arjuna must offer all his actions to Krishna in his mind, regard him as the highest goal, and keep his thoughts always on him, and by his grace, he will cross over all difficulties. But if, out of ego, he will not listen, Krishna warns, he will be lost.

If you cling to your ego, Krishna tells Arjuna, and think that you will not fight, then your resolve is useless, because your own nature will compel you. Bound by the duty born of your nature, he says, you will do even against your will the very thing that confusion makes you wish to avoid. The Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings, causing them all to turn by his power, as if they were mounted on a wheel.

Take refuge in him alone, with your whole being, Krishna says, for by his grace you will reach supreme peace and the eternal home. Thus has he now explained to Arjuna a knowledge more secret than any other secret, he says, and he urges him to think about it fully and then do as he wishes. It is a moving gesture, because the teacher leaves the final decision to the student himself.

Listen again to my supreme word, Krishna says, the most secret of all, for you are dear to me, and so I shall tell you what is good for you. Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, worship me and bow to me, and you will come to me, he promises, and then he adds what many readers call the heart of the whole poem. Let go of every other support and take refuge in me alone, he says, and I will free you from all sin and fear, so do not grieve.

This teaching should never be spoken, Krishna says, to someone who has no discipline, no devotion, no wish to hear it, or who speaks ill of him. The person who teaches this supreme secret to his devotees with devotion will surely come to Krishna, and none among people does him a dearer service. Even the one who studies this sacred conversation or who only hears it with faith, free from envy, is freed and attains the worlds of the righteous.

Krishna asks Arjuna whether he has heard all this with a single mind, and whether his confusion, which was born of ignorance, has been destroyed. Arjuna answers that his confusion is gone and that, by Krishna's grace, he has regained his memory of who he is, that his doubts are removed, and that he will act according to Krishna's word. The man who sat down in despair with his bow cast aside now stands firm.

Sanjaya tells the blind king that he has heard this wonderful conversation between Krishna and the great-souled Arjuna, which makes his hair stand on end. By the grace of the sage Vyasa, he says, he has heard this supreme secret directly from Krishna, the lord of yoga, as he was speaking. Remembering again and again that holy dialogue, and the wonderful form of Krishna, he is amazed and he rejoices again and again.

The Gita ends as it began, with Sanjaya telling the blind king Dhritarashtra that wherever Krishna, the lord of yoga, stands beside Arjuna the archer, there will be good fortune and victory. That is Sanjaya's firm belief, and the poem stops there, before the great battle begins. For readers, it remains what it has been for centuries, a short conversation on a battlefield that has become a long conversation about how to live.
